Quality IMAP, Part 1: Your Mailbox Is A Database

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deuxfleurs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the past year, we have significantly improved the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation.
  • In a recent development, aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures.
  • Implementing an IMAP server is not easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the past year, we have significantly improved the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the first part in a series of blog posts elaborating on why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and the set of techniques we have been using to make our IMAP code as high-quality as we can. In this first part, we focus on one challenging aspect of IMAP: fine-grained retrieval and querying of emails.

In a recent development, aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

Implementing an IMAP server is not easy. Partly because IMAP is an old protocol, with a good number of extensions that has accumulated quite a bit of complexity over time. On top of that IMAP provides - for good reasons - two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents and concurrent multi-client multi-session access to mailboxes.

Sources indicate that this is the first part in a series of posts discussing how we have been approaching IMAP access. In the past year, we have been refining Aerogramme's IMAP implementation to be "more correct", in a context where "correctness" is unfortunately not always well specified: IMAP and email are defined in documents that are often vague, and furthermore, real-world implementations do not always follow specifications.

Today, we'll walk you though our work on the correctness and reliability of Aerogramme for retrieving and querying emails, and explain why your mailbox is, in fact, a database...

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

One challenge of the IMAP specification is the rich feature-set it provides for retrieving mailbox and email contents. We may sometimes think of a mailbox as a directory containing plain email files; however, from the point of view of an IMAP server (or client), a mailbox is closer to a database, accessed using a dedicated query language.

According to recent reports, for instance, mobile clients, which have slower and unreliable connectivity, benefit from fine-grained querying of a mailbox contents. User experience is much better if an email client can selectively fetch the subject of upcoming emails (to update the list of emails in the mailbox) without having to first download all of their attachments or doing a sync of the entire mailbox.

To facilitate the mobile client use-case, IMAP specifies two key mechanisms for querying and (partial) retrieval of emails in a mailbox:.

A direct consequence of these features is that an IMAP server actually needs to parse the emails, not just store them. It then needs to (correctly) interpret the (sometimes tricky) query language of SEARCH and FETCH, and internally support a data architecture that enable efficiently searching and querying over the emails.

Our implementation of SEARCH and FETCH is backed by the three following components:.

According to recent reports, the logic for SEARCH and FETCH is implemented as an interpreter that takes already parsed emails and walks down their AST to evaluate IMAP-specific queries1. This separates email structure (email ASTs do not depend on IMAP concepts) from IMAP-specific business logic. This layer has been significantly reworked in the last months, fixing a good number of logic bugs and edge cases in our implementation of the SEARCH and FETCH IMAP specification.

Email parsing is done using the eml-codec companion library, that we also develop and maintain. The eml-codec library parses emails into a rich, structured AST while also giving access to raw input slices that correspond to relevant AST nodes; this is required for implementing FETCH. In the past year, eml-codec has evolved from an email parsing library with IMAP-specific quirks to a robust, well-tested, general-purpose email library with support for both parsing and printing of emails. You can read more about the library design choices in our work-in-progress design document.

According to recent reports, aerogramme's internal data architecture splits mailbox state, email metadata, and email contents. It is briefly described in Aerogramme's documentation. Mailbox state (emails IDs and flags) and email metadata (parsed headers, date, size) are stored in Aerogramme's metadata storage using Garage K2V, while email contents are stored in blob storage using Garage S3. This allows SEARCH to be efficient by only reading pre-computed information in metadata storage. At the moment there are no other significant optimizations for FETCH/SEARCH; the likely next step would be to add a full-text search engine.

It has been revealed that these components are all quite non-trivial! Let's now talk about the strategies we've deployed to make them as correct as we could.

Industry observers note that we ran our implementation of FETCH and SEARCH through ImapTest: a testing tool for IMAP servers maintained by the Dovecot developers. ImapTest was invaluable in surfacing problems with FETCH and SEARCH, but is equally useful to test all other aspects of IMAP.

Most relevant for FETCH and SEARCH was the test suite provided with ImapTest: a collection of hand-crafted test scenarios testing many subtle or "interesting" aspects of the IMAP specification. Each scenario consists of IMAP commands to send to the server, and a specification of the corresponding expected responses.

Sources indicate that running the ImapTest test suite found a small number of bugs in SEARCH, mostly in edge-cases of the specification. However, testing FETCH revealed that our initial implementation of the BODY[] subcommand was conceptually wrong in many cases! This subcommand of FETCH retrieves a sub-part of an email by following its structure, which we implement by walking down the email's AST. Our initial implementation was done by reading the IMAP specification and interpreting its sometimes vague wording as best as we could; only testing with ImapTest made us realize that our best-guess interpretation was wrong in many cases. More precisely: it did not match ImapTest's reading of the spec, which, in doubt, is what we prefer to follow!

Sources indicate that imapTest was also relatively pleasant to use to do manual "differential testing" for any remaining edge-cases: when we had any doubt, we could easily write additional scenarios and compare Aerogramme's output with Dovecot's; treating Dovecot as an oracle. After a few rounds of bugfixing, Aerogramme's implementation of FETCH and SEARCH is now in much better shape.

According to recent reports, the lesson we learned is that the IMAP specification can leave room for interpretation in surprising ways. In fact, to further illustrate this point, let's talk about one ImapTest scenario that we haven't "fixed" yet in Aerogramme because we just found it very confusing, and we are not sure what to do!

He's a tricky case. SEARCH FROM returns the list of emails whose From header "contains" the given string. Now, what does "contains" mean here, exactly? When running SEARCH FROM foo@example.com on the two following headers, which ones should match?

In a recent development, some additional context on email syntax is useful here: these two email addresses are equivalent. The local-part of the email (before the @) allows quoted strings, so "foo" can be used and simply denotes foo. Email syntax also allows comments in various places; they are written between parentheses. Comments have no formal meaning but are shown by email clients and can be useful; they are sometimes used by mailing-list software to indicate the name of the list. As an example SYMPA emits From headers of the form From: Alice (via Super Friends List) ).

At the moment, Aerogramme implements SEARCH FROM as plain substring search on the text representation of the header: here, the first header matches, but not the second. However, the ImapTest test suite says that both headers should match! So, what does the specification says?

The IMAP specification2 for SEARCH says:.

According to recent reports, hmm, so, what is this "envelope structure"? Reading further:.

Sources indicate that so the FROM field of an email's "envelope structure" contains a structured representation of parsed email addresses. Regarding our two headers above, they are both represented in the envelope structure as:.

Recent findings suggest that what does it mean for this structured value to "contain" the string foo@example.com? Clearly none of the strings in the structure contain foo@example.com, so perhaps instead we should re-print the structure as an email address and do a substring search on that? However, there is not a unique way of printing a given email address, and the IMAP specification does not define any...

We are quite curious to know if IMAP experts have more to say on this point!

In the meantime, our bugfixes for FETCH and SEARCH have been shipped in Aerogramme 0.5.1 (see the release notes for more details), with the exception of two extra fixes shipped in Aerogramme 0.6.

Sources indicate that FETCH and SEARCH operate on the parsed email ASTs produced by eml-codec. How do we ensure that we have correctly implemented all the subtleties of the email format in eml-codec, which is itself described in an old and tricky set of specifications? As often, the answer is: more testing.

Sources indicate that to ensure our implementation is correct, we performed fuzzer-guided Property-Based Testing (PBT) of the email parser and printer in eml-codec. Specifically, we tested the following "roundtrip" property:.

âfor an arbitrary email value in eml-codec's internal AST, printing it then parsing the printed output must yield an equivalent ASTâ.

Industry observers note that the starting AST is generated by a fuzzer as a structured value using the Arbitrary trait; the cargo-fuzz tutorial calls this "Structure-Aware Fuzzing". A roundtrip in the other direction, i.e. "parse then print then test for string equality" would not generally hold, as there are many equivalent ways of printing the same email, for instance because of line folding...

While it may seem that any reasonable implementation would satisfy our roundtrip property, in practice, this methodology immediately surfaced a lot of bugs and edge cases.

The recurring theme was that the fuzzer would generate "exotic" AST values breaking the roundtrip property, for which we had to clarify:.

In the first case, this fixed bugs or potential security concerns for users of the parser (like Aerogramme) or printer. In the second case, it improved the definition of internal AST types, which is relevant when using eml-codec to programatically compose emails, not something we use in Aerogramme itself, but relevant for an experimental mailing-list server project in Deuxfleurs using the same library.

To illustrate the kind of issues that we are talking about here, let's look at an tricky example that was found using our fuzzing methodology.

In a recent development, the "MIME Part Three" specification (RFC2047) specifies a way of using non-ASCII text in selected places of email headers. (Full support for UTF-8 in headers, which eml-codec also supports, was only introduced later.) Where allowed by the specification, ASCII text can be replaced by an "encoded word": an ASCII encoding of non-ASCII text using special syntax introduced by the specification.

As an example, the UTF-8 word aÃ©rogramme can be encoded as follows:.

More generally, a MIME encoded word has the following structure:.

When using the q encoding like above, most ASCII characters can be used directly in the encoded text, and other bytes must be encoded as = followed by their hexadecimal code.

Now, let us consider the following From header:.

Recent findings suggest that this looks like an encoded word followed by some extra junk; is this a valid From header? Perhaps surprisingly, there is no encoded word in this header, and it is a valid email address! The email address is =?utf-8?q? @ [?= X] (it is technically valid!), where the part after the '@' uses the uncommon "domain-literal" syntax.

Now, consider the following Subject header with the same byte representation:.

This time, the first part of the header is an encoded word, and the whole header tells us that the subject is the string @[ X]!

The explanation for this behavior follows from the specification (which is fairly clear on this aspect): the set of ASCII characters that can be used unescaped in depends on the context in which the encoded word appears.

In a recent development, encoded words can appear in From headers (for example From: =?utf-8?q?a=C3=A9rogramme?= is valid), but in that context they cannot use @ or [ unescaped, which is why the first example does not in fact contain a valid encoded word. In the context of a Subject header, the set of valid unescaped characters is broader and includes both @ and [, making =?utf-8?q?@[?= is a valid encoded word representing the string @[.

To implement this behavior, we needed to correctly track the context in which we parse encoded words, "tokenize" them according to that context, and also track context sensitivity in our email AST and during printing. Getting every detail to align properly between parsing, our internal AST, and printing took us several attempts! In that process, our property-testing setup was extremely useful, as it could quickly come up with fresh convoluted examples like the one above that revealed bugs in edge cases of our code.

The lesson here is that email specifications can be quite complicated and tricky to implement, even when they are clear! And, in our experience, without automatic test generation (like our fuzzer setup), it is very hard to manually come up with examples that actually cover edge cases...

If you want to see more details, the bulk of our PBT/fuzzing work on eml-codec was done in eml-codec 0.3 and shipped in Aerogramme 0.4, with some additional improvements shipped in Aerogramme 0.6.

We tested eml-codec on collections of real-world emails (more than 100k emails) to evaluate and improve the recovery strategies of eml-codec's parser on invalid or broken syntax.

Many legitimate emails found in the real world are, indeed, incorrect with respect to email specifications. Often, the use of invalid or broken syntax is local (to specific headers, or parts of a header); in some cases, it is "only" a minor deviation from the specification.

The case of "message IDs" can be taken as an example. Emails can be given an identifier (specified using the Message-ID header) so that later emails can reference it (using the In-Reply-To and References headers). This is useful to display email "threads" in email clients, for example. The message ID syntax is also used to identify attachments with the Content-ID header.

Reading the specification, a message ID is of the form:.

and a list of message IDs as used by In-Reply-To and References separates message IDs with whitespace:.

The specification also documents that, for the list syntax, "obsolete" syntax (that we must support) can include extra text surrounding message IDs...

Now, what do we find in our sample of real-world emails?

-> Emitted by apple-mail, and invalid: no @!

-> Invalid: no angle brackets !

-> Valid: an instance of the "obsolete" syntax documented by the specification.

-> Commas are valid as part of the obsolete syntax, but the second message-id is malformed because of incorrect line folding (\n\t) in the middle of a word.

Industry observers note that the consequence is that eml-codec needs to be able to recover from broken syntax: on an email containing invalid syntax, it should be able to discard the broken parts and parse as much as it can from the rest of the email, instead of simply returning an error. It should also ideally be able to parse invalid but common deviations from the specifications in order to recover information instead of discarding them.

It has been revealed that we first extended eml-codec with coarse-grained recovery strategies, such as discarding an entire header field if we couldn't parse it. This allowed us to quickly reach a state where the eml-codec parser is a total function: for any input bytes, it always returns an email AST representing an RFC-compliant email3, discarding any part of the input it does not understand.

It has been revealed that we then instrumented the parser to log each time it discards broken input when recovering, and ran the instrumented parser on the email that we collected. This gave us a lot of examples of legitimate emails with broken syntax. In each case, then, we manually looked at the piece of broken syntax, see if we could make some sense of it, and decide whether:.

This whole process was particularly interesting because it made us face the many subtleties of real-world emails (sometimes far from the "truth" of specifications); eml-codec is now much more robust operating on real-world emails!

According to recent reports, this methodology involves a lot of tradeoffs and judgment calls: there is a limit to the amount of parsing hacks that we can add in terms of code quality but also parsing ambiguity; and some classes of emails are more critical than others (e.g. we should not spend too much effort supporting spam emails). A strong design constraint of eml-codec is that, up to a few exceptions, we want its internal AST to only represent RFC-compliant emails, so we did not want to pollute it to include random broken syntax just for the sake of "recovering more". The whole process, in particular, helped us clarify the design of eml-codec as a library.

According to recent reports, for more details, you can look at the release notes of eml-codec 0.3.1 where the bulk of the work is done, building on eml-codec 0.2 for the initial setup of parsing recovery. Both shipped with Aerogramme 0.4.

IMAP's search and retrieval features are essential because they allow clients to have a snappy UX while handling mailboxes with thousands of emails. This post focused on getting those basic features right. But, more broadly, we think that the "mailbox as database" perspective is useful because it raises the question: which end-user workflows can we enable and support? Which features should we prioritize or optimize to best support the workflows of day-to-day email users?

Stay tuned for the next blogpost in the series where we discuss the other significant challenge for an IMAP server: mailbox concurrency!

Following the database analogy, the logical next step could be to optimize this by first "pre-compiling" queries before running them on emails. Right now we don't know if this optimization would actually matter in practice...

This links to IMAP4rev1 but the more recent IMAP4rev2 isn't more specific on this subject.

The current eml-codec AST has a few selected exceptions to this rule, where it allows representing non-compliant data in well identified cases. One of such cases is non-compliant message IDs, such as message IDs without @...

Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Alpine Linux Owners Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw.
  • Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.
  • In a recent development, the flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Alpine Linux Owners Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw.

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.

In a recent development, the flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call. On an affected system, a password longer than 256 bytes causes musl to return an error value. That value is an asterisk, the same character Linux uses in /etc/shadow to mark an account as having no password. OpenSSH then treats the returned asterisk as a match and permits the login.

Recent findings suggest that the conditions to exploit the vulnerability are however quite narrow. The server must run OpenSSH before version 10.6p2, be built against the musl library rather than glibc, and operate without PAM. It must also have at least one account with a SHA-256 or SHA-512 password hash and another account marked with an asterisk in its shadow entry. When those conditions are met, any password between 257 and 1,024 characters can authenticate against the passwordless account.

Alpine Linux is the most prominent distribution affected, as it uses musl and its default OpenSSH configuration does not enable PAM. Other musl-based environments, including OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto, may also be affected where the same configuration applies. Systems using glibc, PAM, Dropbear or OpenBSD are not affected.

According to recent reports, ozgun Kultekin, a security researcher at Wakefield, published the technical explanation on the *sshole site. Kultekin traces the problem to two musl changes made in 2012: the first replaced the NULL error return from crypt() with an asterisk, and the second added a 256-byte limit to SHA-512 password hashing, so longer inputs caused an error. Together, the changes produced a value that could be mistaken for a password hash.

Sources indicate that the OpenSSH side of the problem dates from a 2016 fix for CVE-2016-6210, which was a timing attack that could reveal whether a username existed. To make responses take a similar amount of time for valid and invalid consumers, OpenSSH borrowed the salt from another account and hashed the supplied password anyway. That workaround also applied to real accounts whose shadow entry contained an asterisk.

According to recent reports, kultekin writes that the problem remained unnoticed for roughly a decade because the vulnerable combination was uncommon in testing. OpenSSH is tested on OpenBSD and glibc-based systems, while many Linux distributions route authentication through PAM, which does not call crypt() for asterisk entries in the same way. Kultekin states the bug was found after building OpenSSH in several configurations and testing about 17,600 unusual login attempts.

Industry observers note that on Alpine's official AWS and Azure images, the default alpine user is marked as passwordless and can use doas without a password. This means that an attacker who reaches that account can therefore obtain root privileges. Dan Goodin reports for Ars Technica that the issue can give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts within seconds on affected systems.

In a recent development, openSSH 10.6p2 contains a fix. Operators who cannot upgrade immediately can disable password authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no in the SSH server configuration and restarting sshd. Kultekin also advises checking authentication logs for evidence that an account with no password accepted a password. The project has published a detection and background repository.

In a recent development, the vulnerability is being actively exploited. Goodin notes that GreyNoise reported that honeypots in Southeast Asia had been attacked by a group it is tracking known as GT10, which reportedly deploys a backdoor which supports shell commands, reconnaissance and persistence. Goodin reports that watchTowr linked the activity to botnets and cryptocurrency operations, while Previdian recorded 20 exploitation attempts from 13 IP addresses in nine countries. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 November, according to Hackread.

Red Hat has stated that its products are not affected because they do not meet the required combination of musl and no PAM. Amazon has likewise marked Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 as not affected. That does not remove the risk for teams running Alpine-based containers, embedded devices or custom musl builds. Administrators should look for SSH servers built against musl, check whether PAM is disabled, review shadow entries for asterisk-locked accounts, apply OpenSSH 10.6p2 and restart the service.

Industry observers note that the vulnerability was publicly disclosed on 5 November and exploitation reports followed within days. For organisations with internet-facing SSH services, the immediate action to take is fairly straightforward: upgrade OpenSSH, restart it, and remove password authentication where it is not needed.

Tech Report: Up to 3.2x Faster Inference with LFM2.5-DSpark

📅 20 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B.
  • Recent findings suggest that the decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound.
  • Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:.

Recent findings suggest that the decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.

According to recent reports, we follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

In a recent development, under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

In a recent development, we measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:.

It has been revealed that then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

Recent findings suggest that the block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:.

We can’t wait to see what you build.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence.
  • Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Critical orgs around the globe under seige.

Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence.

Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks.

In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys.

“Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday.

Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, Latest API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama.

This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models.

In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks.

“The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote.

The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt.

In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses remarked is “close to what a live video check expects.”.

Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image.

Sources indicate that while the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote.

None of the attack techniques are latest, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker.

Recent findings suggest that “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.”.

The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.”.

Industry observers note that the federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants.

After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October.

According to recent reports, however, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI.

The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert.

These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®.

#10832. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

📅 21 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels.
  • One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice.
  • However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was remarked, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

According to recent reports, for example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

Sources indicate that when we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a upcoming parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

In a recent development, the reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Voice clone of the same speaker.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff.

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

Industry observers note that the results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

According to recent reports, models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

Industry observers note that to build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

In a recent development, some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:.

2011 draft budget (masked numbers).

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Sources indicate that our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11.

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11.

According to recent reports, within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister.".

Recent findings suggest that multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

It has been revealed that other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that for people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to upcoming audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that openAI released a study on November 16, 2026, covering 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 academic scientists and survey responses from 251 participants.
  • End-to-end autonomous research, defined as requests for AI to coordinate literature review, ideation and downstream analysis, accounted for only 0.4% of the average scientist’s scientific messages.
  • The full paper analyzes activity from August 20 through September 22, 2026, and a survey conducted September 30 to October 7, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that openAI released a study on November 16, 2026, covering 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 academic scientists and survey responses from 251 participants. It examines how the scientists used ChatGPT and Codex across research work and how they expect AI to affect discovery.

End-to-end autonomous research, defined as requests for AI to coordinate literature review, ideation and downstream analysis, accounted for only 0.4% of the average scientist’s scientific messages. Yet 15.3% of scientists sent at least one such request, a gap the paper interprets as experimentation with full automation rather than routine use.

The full paper analyzes activity from August 20 through September 22, 2026, and a survey conducted September 30 to October 7, 2026. Researchers used privacy-preserving classifiers to categorize messages without reading the underlying exchanges, and program data were not used for model training by default.

Reading and knowledge acquisition accounted for 27.7% of the average scientist’s scientific messages, while writing and communication represented 26.9%. Scientific analysis contributed 16.7% and research software and code development 13.8%; together, those four workflows represented 85%.

According to recent reports, that concentration puts most current AI use in discrete knowledge-work tasks rather than coordinated research projects. Explaining scientific concepts was the leading individual task at 18.8% of messages, with 89.7% of scientists sending at least three such requests.

Ideation tells a different story about breadth. It represented 5.3% of messages, but about 68% of scientists sent at least three ideation messages during the study. Across those messages, scientists supplied a specific question 35% of the time, asked ChatGPT to refine an existing idea 36% of the time, and asked it to suggest a research question 23% of the time. The remaining 6% could not be categorized.

The paper also identifies a stage-dependent division of labor. Scientists often asked AI to propose directions during early exploration, then supplied their own questions or ideas for refinement when developing specific research problems.

Sources indicate that the paper’s scientist-involvement score, measuring the average share of initial requests followed by clarification, checking or revision, was 31.8%. Writing and communication had the highest score at 38.0%, followed by scientific analysis at 34.4% and research software at 33.7%.

For comparable tasks, requests requiring advanced or frontier expertise had higher involvement in 28 of 32 cases, by an average of 6.5 percentage points. More specialized work therefore generally drew more follow-up, not less.

Sources indicate that the score considers only the next scientific message in the same conversation within seven days and does not capture revisions made outside the AI application. Checking or correcting outputs was also the most commonly selected difficulty in obtaining value from ChatGPT, chosen by 45.4% of surveyed scientists.

Those review demands coexist with self-reported time savings. Across eight research activities, surveyed scientists estimated that one hour of work with AI would have taken about 1.9 hours without it at the same quality. Reported productivity ratios ranged from 1.36 times for administration to 2.85 times for research software and code development.

Industry observers note that expectations for discovery were also high. Of the 250 scientists answering the discovery-timeline question, 98% expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field. Asked to imagine a discovery that would take ten years without AI, 72.0% expected it at least three years sooner with AI, including 21.6% who expected it within three years.

Written explanations emphasized execution over full automation. Among 367 reasons identified in 224 responses, 52% concerned faster research execution, while automating research loops accounted for 2.2%. Another 23% concerned finding more promising research questions and 14% pursuing a wider range of questions.

Recent findings suggest that the reported bottlenecks extend beyond model capability. Limited time or staffing was selected by 51.8% of respondents and limited funding by 43.8%; validating or reproducing findings affected 25.5%, while access to equipment, laboratories or computing resources affected 24.3%.

Industry observers note that openAI cautions that participants were a selected group who applied for expanded AI access and chose to answer an AI survey, so the results may not generalize to all scientists. Usage shares describe requests rather than research value or time allocation, and the findings do not establish causal effects.

Alongside the study, OpenAI confirmed an expansion of ChatGPT for Academic Researchers, saying the pilot had reached 20,000 researchers in 33 countries since July 2026.

In a recent development, applications for 50,000 latest grants open November 23, 2026, on a first-come, first-served basis for eligible researchers, replacing the pilot’s lottery-based selection. Each grant covers a recipient and up to two collaborators with free ChatGPT Plus access, supporting as many as 150,000 researchers in this round. OpenAI’s goal is to reach 200,000 researchers across the program.

OpenAI noted Plus replaced ChatGPT Pro for the new grants because most pilot usage would have remained within Plus limits.

The expansion broadens access to the tools, but the study’s central implication concerns the work around them: whether time saved on individual tasks survives the checking scientists still perform and the staffing, funding and experimental constraints they report.

Sources indicate that jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

It has been revealed that with a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

📅 21 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, 3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet).
  • Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can swiftly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.
  • Industry observers note that it's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, 3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can swiftly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

Industry observers note that it's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

It has been revealed that for Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:.

It has been revealed that today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:.

Sources indicate that the expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

According to recent reports, we avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:.

For each vector generation, we record:.

Sources indicate that our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 newly introduced features:.

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:.

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:.

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:.

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

This gives us several useful properties:.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the newly introduced generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

In a recent development, batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

Industry observers note that we deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:.

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:.

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Owners still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

In a recent development, for every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):.

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​.

Recent findings suggest that RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Sources indicate that dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:.

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

According to recent reports, the large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. Upcoming papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Recent findings suggest that launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

It has been revealed that each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:.

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

It has been revealed that corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

In a recent development, the revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

It has been revealed that scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Sources indicate that matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

According to recent reports, upcoming generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

TensorWave expects to bring the first capacity online in the first half of 2027 and complete the full deployment by early 2028. This infrastructure is intended to support both large-scale training and inference.

It has been revealed that the company describes the agreement as its largest deployment to date and a significant expansion of its U.S. infrastructure footprint. Industry observers note that tensorWave says it is the first publicly revealed specialist AI-cloud provider supporting that collaboration. The arrangement adds an infrastructure operator to a partnership previously framed around the chip supplier and model developer.

TensorWave says it was the first public cloud to deploy AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs, later expanded across MI325X and MI355X hardware, and now operates one of the world’s largest AMD-exclusive AI clouds and one of North America’s largest AMD-based AI training clusters. TensorWave reports having secured more than 2 gigawatts of long-term data-center capacity, providing a broader base for its U.S. expansion. The OpenAI contract makes execution the immediate measure of that pipeline: TensorWave must turn its AMD operating experience and secured capacity into reliable single-tenant infrastructure across several sites on the confirmed timetable. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, most interesting AI apps are pipelines.
  • Sources indicate that gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface.
  • According to recent reports, the best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

Sources indicate that gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

According to recent reports, the best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Recent findings suggest that upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

👉 Try the Image Editor Pipeline.

Sources indicate that one graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Industry observers note that each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

Recent findings suggest that you get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

It has been revealed that every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Recent findings suggest that check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Sources indicate that every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:.

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:.

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:.

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

It has been revealed that you can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering.

Nov 16, 2026 3 min read.

According to recent reports, the Uno Platform team released Uno Platform 7.0, which unifies rendering on SkiaSharp 4 with an experimental WebGPU backend, adds Apple TV as a target platform and supports .NET 11 from day zero. The release also brings third-party .NET MAUI controls and Microsoft.UI.Reactor library to every target, and removes native rendering and Mac Catalyst.

Recent findings suggest that uno Platform is an open-source framework for building .NET applications with C# and WinUI XAML for Windows, Android, iOS, macOS, Linux and WebAssembly. The team describes 7.0 as its largest release, with 5,219 commits and 704 closed concerns since 6.7. According to the team’s benchmarks, 7.0 is about 2x faster at the median and 5x smaller than 6.7, with some operations, such as brush creation, up to 38x faster. These figures come from the vendor and the workloads were not published in detail.

All targets now render through one pluggable pipeline. SkiaSharp 4 is the default, and Uno Platform is a co-maintainer of the library alongside the .NET team at Microsoft. On Android, Windows and Linux, Skia now renders through Vulkan by default. The WebGPU backend, available on all desktop, mobile and WebAssembly targets, is enabled by adding WebGpu to UnoFeatures and registering the backend on the host builder. It uses wgpu-native outside the browser and the browser’s own WebGPU support on WebAssembly. The team measured up to a 50% frame-rate improvement depending on the scene, and indicates a WebGPU-only app drops about 6 MB of uncompressed native code from WebAssembly builds. A newly introduced WebGpuCanvasElement lets applications glitch their own WebGPU commands inside the UI.

Industry observers note that through .NET MAUI Embedding, controls from vendors such as Syncfusion, Telerik, Infragistics, DevExpress and Esri previously ran only on iOS, Android, macOS and Windows. They now work on every Uno Platform target, including the web and Linux. In the other direction, existing .NET MAUI apps can reach the browser and Linux through Uno Platform’s .NET MAUI handlers.

According to recent reports, microsoft.UI.Reactor, Microsoft’s declarative C# framework for WinUI with hooks such as UseState and no XAML, now runs on desktop, browser, Android and iOS. It is enabled with the Reactor UnoFeature, is in preview, and can coexist with existing XAML pages in the same visual tree. Apple TV support is added through the net10.0-tvos target framework, targets tvOS 15 and later, renders through Metal and uses the Siri Remote for focus navigation. .NET 11 is supported on every head, for example through dotnet newly introduced unoapp -tfm net11.0, while .NET 10 remains the long-term support option.

RichTextBlock and RichEditBox are now available on every platform, closing an concern opened in 2018. WinUI alignment continues with ItemsRepeater and ItemsView ported from current WinUI sources, LinedFlowLayout, the TitleBar control, multiple windows on iPad and Lottie rendering through Composition. Smaller additions include built-in input validation through INotifyDataErrorInfo, TalkBack, VoiceOver and AT-SPI screen-reader support, and the uno-devserver app command for launching and inspecting running apps from scripts and CI.

Industry observers note that most apps upgrade by changing the Uno.Sdk version in global.json, following the migration guide. The team released Uno Platform Studio 3.3 alongside it.

In a recent development, the release follows Uno Platform 6.7 in September, which added Android TV, Android Auto and Wear OS targets, semantic styles shared by the Material and Simple themes, and damage-region repainting on Skia renderers. It also removed the WPF targets.

#10825. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original
