📖 Baca

Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost.
  • Industry observers note that our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it?
  • Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Industry observers note that our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

It has been revealed that an alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

According to recent reports, QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

Recent findings suggest that this reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

Industry observers note that there is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below reveals.

Recent findings suggest that to make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

According to recent reports, the two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

Sources indicate that the 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Recent findings suggest that both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

Recent findings suggest that the practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

It has been revealed that the accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

Recent findings suggest that the takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

Recent findings suggest that this work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

According to recent reports, want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Recent findings suggest that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Industry observers note that this is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—crucial capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡.

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

It has been revealed that I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Sources indicate that definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠.

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other.".

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section indicates the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

Industry observers note that the comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

In a recent development, we don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for women, the need and desire to nurture each other is not pathological but redemptive, and it is within that knowledge that our real power I rediscovered.
  • According to recent reports, the open software ecosystem is not in a good way.
  • Industry observers note that the Licensing of the Press Act 1662 in England was drafted in the wake of the printing press to provide publishers with a monopoly on printing registered books.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for women, the need and desire to nurture each other is not pathological but redemptive, and it is within that knowledge that our real power I rediscovered. It is this real connection which is so feared by a patriarchal world. Only within a patriarchal structure is maternity the only social power open to women.

According to recent reports, the open software ecosystem is not in a good way. We’ve seen escalating abuse of our commons by the very entities we were trying to provide an alternative to. Our default tool against this, copyleft, is repeatedly showing itself incapable of rising to these challenges. understandably, many find it difficult to see a path forward. In this context, many are attempting to double down on copyleft, with some even going as far as making their work proprietary in an attempt to maintain control of how it’s used. Herein I hope to share a different vision.

Industry observers note that the Licensing of the Press Act 1662 in England was drafted in the wake of the printing press to provide publishers with a monopoly on printing registered books. Its purpose was to protect publishers from competition, ensuring their profitability, and to provide a means for censorship. Notably unrepresented in this consideration are authors, who could not register books themselves. The act was temporary, and in 1694, unable to secure a continuation from parliament, publishers were in need of a new approach. It was only then that they chose to highlight authors’ rights, to make the proposed legislation palatable to a public tiring of their greed. Yet, they did this knowing that even with authors holding these rights, they could do little with them other than sell them straight back to the publishers from a disadvantaged bargaining position.

According to recent reports, that’s not to say we haven’t had our wins. Copyleft was a big one. But I’m reminded of Lorde’s wisdom:.

Those of us who stand outside the circle of this society’s definition of acceptable women; those of us who have been forged in the crucibles of difference—those of us who are poor, who are lesbians, who are Black, who are older—know that survival is not an academic skill. It is learning how to take our differences and make them strengths. For the master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house. They may allow us temporarily to beat him at his own game, but they will never enable us to bring about genuine change. And this fact is only threatening to those women who still define the master’s house as their only source of support.

Industry observers note that lorde’s advice is to take our differences and make them strengths. I think there’s more to that I haven’t seen how to apply to our trade yet, but I can at least take a superficial reading:.

I remember as a child my parents were paranoid that my sister or I might get tattoos or unconventional piercings. This wasn’t because they had any particular dislike or prejudice toward such things, or even that they were worried about discrimintation or prejudice from individuals. Their worry instead was that it might make us “unemployable”. We routinely cut off parts of ourselves, to make us generic and palatable enough to be fed into the maw of industry, and we advise others to do the same. I’m not sure I can advise everyone to stop cold turkey in good conscience, as most of us do still rely on an employer to make sure we’re fed and housed, but I’m not willing to do it to myself outside that context, and even within it I find it necessary to push back on some of the conventions of professionalism. I’m definitely not willing to do it to others.

Industry observers note that I’d like to praise Soatok for the example he’s set for me on this front. He’s talked before about regularly getting complaints that his blog is too “unprofessional” to share at work and, like, good. Fuck your manufacturer.

If you don’t want your project used by a firm, filling it with personality seem a more promising way to achieve that than a license. Of course it’s not perfect, your work can always be whitewashed, but if the roots go deep enough those stains can be hard to shake. In any case, it’s more work for the company downstream, especially if they want to track your changes.

Who would have guessed a decade ago that sarcastic commenters on Reddit would be such a big stumbling block for LLM training.

It has been revealed that I recently had to implement OIDC auth in a Rust service at work, and so had the pleasure of dealing with the trait soup that is the openidconnect crate. It crossed my mind that I could write a better version of this crate, or at the very least some more serviceable documentation. Judging by what others have to say in the crate’s issues, there’s demand for it, so I’d be scratching my own itch and helping other programmers out. Myself of even a couple of years ago would have done it. What I wouldn’t have stopped to consider then is why we’re being asked to implement this protocol, and who is served by the protocol becoming easier to implement. It’s a tool for centralisation, lock-in, and surveillance, and I really don’t need to do Google’s legwork for them. Every bit of extra friction in using it is a good thing, in hindsight even my struggles were good. The extra implementation time is a cost my employer paid for making a bad decision, and the compile time burden of all those traits is another cost they will continue to pay until they rip the feature out. If the openidconnect crate didn’t exist, they probably would have given up on the feature entirely.

According to recent reports, it’s not always possible to know how a technology will be used before it exists, but we can make some pretty good guesses. A technology like BitTorrent functions to advance freedom of information, and because that purpose is set so clearly in it’s structure, it has proved resistant to subversion. Indeed it seems resistant to attempts to do anything else but share information, including its creator’s attempts to monetise it.

According to recent reports, this is not a only a hobby for most of us, but also how we sustain ourselves. An undercurrent in the complaints about the state of open software is that it’s hard to make a living writing open software, but I think that’s somewhat by design. The thing we came here to oppose was the control companies exert on the use and development of their software, and the externalities that exerts on the consumers; they do this mostly as a means to extract money. If we were to turn our goal towards extracting money, it would indeed make sense to start exerting more control on the use and development of our software, but at that point we have to question why we’re here and not in a startup lab.

According to recent reports, the old advice to have a day job and do this on the side still carries weight, but I dream of a world where sustenance is not synonymous with profit. I don’t see why I shouldn’t be able to write software that benefits others, and have others do work that benefits me, without either feeling the need to control and capture. We have achieved that within software, but I can’t eat software.

When most people today hear “mutual aid”, they think of charity, and charity is often an ugly thing. Those with many resources “giving” some away to those with few, to ease the suffering caused by their lack of resources, while ignoring the reality that the lack of resources is often solely due to enclosure of the resources by those with many. It offers no real answer to the injustice it purports to address, and instead primarily functions to assuage the guilt of the perpetrators, and give them an excuse to avoid having to contend with the root of the problem. We can do better.

Industry observers note that mutual aid is about seeing systems that produce bad outcomes and working together, whether we are directly affected by those systems or not, to address those outcomes systemically. It is about involving those “in need” (which includes you and your need to eat) in how those needs are met. There are people out there doing things you need, with expertise you don’t have, who would benefit from some software help. The connections you build with this kind of work often turn out to be worth more than a paycheck, and it gives you a chance to practice making software that molds to its people’ needs rather than the reverse, which has given me a needed ray of sunshine amid the bleak outlook this industry engenders on our profession.

The Inference Economics Scorecard Challenges GPU Utilization as an AI Performance Metric

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A busy GPU is not necessarily a productive GPU.
  • According to recent reports, the framework shifts attention from chip activity to useful output delivered within a service target, measured against electricity, rack space, and cost.
  • Alongside the announcement, WEKA is highlighting an eight-hour benchmark conducted with Nebius on NVIDIA HGX B300 hardware and releasing workload traces and tooling for others to reproduce the comparison.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A busy GPU is not necessarily a productive GPU. That is the argument behind The Inference Economics Scorecard, new research from NAND Research and WEKA that proposes a broader way to judge the infrastructure running production AI.

According to recent reports, the framework shifts attention from chip activity to useful output delivered within a service target, measured against electricity, rack space, and cost. Its relevance grows as AI agents maintain long conversations, call tools, and return repeatedly to earlier context. An inference server can spend substantial compute rebuilding that context while its utilization dashboard still looks healthy.

Alongside the announcement, WEKA is highlighting an eight-hour benchmark conducted with Nebius on NVIDIA HGX B300 hardware and releasing workload traces and tooling for others to reproduce the comparison. The scorecard is a proposed evaluation framework, rather than an established industry standard. WEKA, whose storage technology benefits from this framing, sponsored the research.

Inference is the process of running a trained model to produce an answer. Before generating new tokens, the model processes the input and conversation history in a phase called prefill. During that work, it creates a key-value cache, or KV cache: intermediate attention data that lets it reuse earlier computation when the conversation continues.

Recent findings suggest that the fastest place for that cache is the GPU’s high-bandwidth memory, known as HBM. But HBM must also accommodate model weights and other working data. Long sessions and competing consumers can force a server to evict cached context to make room.

When the user or agent returns, the missing cache may have to be rebuilt by processing old tokens again. This does not mean the model has permanently lost the conversation. It means the infrastructure has discarded a reusable representation and must pay to reconstruct it.

Industry observers note that that creates a measurement trap. Reprocessing yesterday’s context keeps the GPU active, just as generating a useful newly introduced answer does. Utilization remains a valuable diagnostic signal, but cannot by itself tell an operator how much productive work customers received.

The scorecard calls for continuous tests lasting at least eight hours, long enough to expose behavior that short demonstrations may miss. Comparisons must hold the model, precision, workload, concurrency, cache conditions, quality threshold, and service-level objectives constant. The measurement boundary covers the serving stack, with cooling and facility overhead disclosed.

Recent findings suggest that only successful output meeting the quality and service targets contributes to useful throughput. Failed requests, retries, timeouts, and discarded output must remain visible rather than disappearing from the calculation.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction between throughput and goodput is especially crucial. A server that produces more tokens but misses a customer’s response deadline can be less useful than a slower-looking system that consistently meets it. Similarly, a larger cache is only economically attractive if its benefit exceeds the additional storage, networking, and operating expense.

Sources indicate that WEKA’s technical account of the benchmark describes NeuralMesh with Augmented Memory Grid, which keeps reusable KV data on shared NVMe storage beyond the GPU’s own memory. NVMe is a high-performance interface commonly used with flash drives.

Sources indicate that in this design, the cache becomes a resource the serving infrastructure can retrieve across the network, instead of repeatedly reconstructing it on a GPU. RDMA, or remote direct memory access, and NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage help move data along a direct storage-to-GPU path with less CPU involvement.

Industry observers note that this is a trade between moving existing data and recomputing it. A sufficiently fast storage path can make retrieval cheaper than rebuilding long histories. The advantage depends on cache reuse, context length, concurrency, and the speed of the entire data path; a short request whose working data already fits in HBM presents a different problem.

It has been revealed that the joint Nebius and WEKA test used one eight-GPU HGX B300 serving node running DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Its replay workload drew on more than 5,000 real agent traces, maintained a pool of 512 active sessions, and used a scheduler permitting 32 concurrent requests. Active sessions and simultaneous requests are different measures.

It has been revealed that across eight hours, WEKA reports 3.7 times more output tokens per GPU-hour with its shared cache than with HBM-only serving. Among successfully completed requests, 97% reached a first token within five seconds, compared with 44% for the baseline. Recomputing previously encountered context consumed 60% of prefill cycles in the baseline, versus 6.8% with the shared cache.

Recent findings suggest that the additional cache used NVMe drives across an eight-node cluster, even though the reported serving result came from one GPU node. The GPU-normalized gain therefore does not establish an equivalent reduction in total cost or energy: those calculations must include the supporting resources.

In a recent development, the baseline also matters. The technical write-up indicates a suitable DRAM-offload implementation for this model was unavailable when testing took place. These results compare the tested configuration with HBM-only serving, rather than proving superiority over every alternative cache architecture.

WEKA’s open-source kvlab project captures and replays the structure of agent sessions, including timing and cache-reuse patterns, without distributing the original conversation or source-code content. Its loader is documented in NVIDIA’s AIPerf tooling, and the announcement also identifies integration with SemiAnalysis’s AgentX benchmark.

Preserving pauses, growing histories, and related agent activity helps expose cache pressure that a stream of unrelated synthetic prompts would overlook. Such replays measure serving behavior; they do not by themselves demonstrate whether an agent completed a business task correctly.

Recent findings suggest that for enterprises, the central contribution of The Inference Economics Scorecard is a clearer definition of success: useful responses, at the required quality and speed, within the resources available. As agents consume more context and run for longer, keeping a GPU busy becomes a starting observation. What matters commercially is the work that reaches the customer.

Granite 4.2 LLMs: How They're Built

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.
  • TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B.
  • Granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

The three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split shows up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:.

Granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

Sources indicate that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

The agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

We apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

In a recent development, we then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

Finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

The complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

According to recent reports, before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:.

It has been revealed that for the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

The 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

In a recent development, after SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

According to recent reports, figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

Every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single update behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

In a recent development, advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

The pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:.

What changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:.

Recent findings suggest that parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

In a recent development, the KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:.

Sources indicate that the 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

Recent findings suggest that A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:.

Industry observers note that verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

Each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:.

Boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

In the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

Sources indicate that figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

Reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

Sources indicate that figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

Sources indicate that granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

In a recent development, figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

Figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

According to recent reports, we also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

Industry observers note that the FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

According to recent reports, the NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

Several GGUF formats are provided:.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:.

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

The training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

Granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Recent findings suggest that granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

OpenCode is an AI coding agent that runs in your terminal.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Baseten declared the Voice Agent Stack and Baseten Realtime Voice on November 16, 2026, opening both to private preview through a waitlist and reporting roughly one-second median turn latency across up to 56 concurrent sessions in its test setup. The stack co-locates speech models and orchestration, lets customers choose models independently and scales each pipeline component separately.

The Voice Agent Stack runs on Baseten Dedicated Inference, placing the orchestrator and models in one cloud region over an in-cluster network. Baseten remarked a remote orchestrator can add hundreds of milliseconds of network round trips per turn even when the speech-to-text, language and text-to-speech components are all hosted on its platform. The stack also supplies inference-runtime optimization, inter-model networking, traffic autoscaling, cross-cloud failover and model post-training support.

Industry observers note that realtime Voice is the reference implementation, running a cascade of Baseten-optimized open-weight models for speech-to-text, language processing and text-to-speech with a custom Pipecat-based orchestrator. Its optional delegation design keeps a fast, co-located talker model handling conversation while a stronger external thinker model asynchronously manages reasoning, web search, decisions and tool calls. Server-side tools execute on the co-located orchestrator, which can also call remote Model Context Protocol servers, avoiding extra client round trips; client-side tools are supported as well.

It has been revealed that customers can choose the speech-to-text, language and text-to-speech models independently, combine dedicated components with third-party APIs and move individual pieces onto dedicated infrastructure over time. Post-training options include adapting transcription to industry jargon, tuning language-model behavior for calls and supervised fine-tuning of speech with a customer’s voice data. A session can switch its language model, voice or transcription route without redeployment.

Sources indicate that the API matches the core OpenAI Realtime event protocol and supports audio-in/audio-out and text-in/audio-out modes, alongside transcription keyword boosting, configurable acknowledgments and voice cloning. Compatibility has practical limits: clients must accept a full WebSocket URL. OpenAI’s Python SDK cannot connect directly because it appends /realtime to its base URL, a path Baseten’s endpoint does not serve. Browser clients need a backend to hold the API key and relay the socket because browsers cannot set the required Authorization header.

In a recent development, baseten reported median time to first audio rising from 0.94 seconds with one concurrent call to 1.14 seconds at 56. The latency tests used contexts up to 16,000 tokens; longer contexts can raise turn latency, while configurable summarization can hold each session to a target context length. The test configuration used Qwen3-ASR on one RTX-6000, Gemma-4-31B on one B200, Qwen3-TTS on another RTX-6000 and GLM-5.3 Fast through Baseten Model APIs for delegation.

It has been revealed that each component scales independently against its own concurrency target, allowing operators to add capacity to the stage that saturates instead of duplicating the full pipeline. The design is intended to preserve strict p90 and p95 latency tails while keeping GPU utilization high. Baseten estimated $0.012 per audio minute at 32 concurrent sessions, excluding the per-token cost of reasoning-model delegation, and $0.008 per call-minute at 56 sessions including Model API delegation, under its stated utilization assumptions. Dedicated pricing amortizes hardware across additional sessions, making sustained utilization central to those economics.

An independent speech-to-text benchmark from Coval provides component-level context. Its 24-hour leaderboard, with data timestamped 17:30 UTC on November 16, 2026, ranked Baseten-hosted Qwen3 ASR 1.7b second by median Time to Final Segment at 33 milliseconds, with a 2.1% word error rate over 456 samples. The metric starts at a shared end-of-speech point and ends when the final transcript arrives, excluding the time a live system spends detecting that the turn has ended. It therefore does not measure the full agent response.

Industry observers note that baseten mentioned future work includes more complex orchestration flows, easier migration of existing voice pipelines, native speech-to-speech full-duplex systems, omni models with dedicated speech-generation heads and new scheduling primitives across the cascade. The launch makes orchestration the control point for voice-agent economics: model choice, tool execution and component-level capacity are handled together, giving operators several ways to tune latency and GPU use without rebuilding the full pipeline.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.
  • AWS has rolled out Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field.

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.

AWS has rolled out Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor. On Amazon EKS, the whole change is one pod field: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.

In a recent development, the feature is available in all commercial regions at no additional charge, and AWS positions it for workloads where the tenant or the code cannot be trusted, with coding agents named first. In an AWS blog post, Carlos Santana and Trishi Mehta write:.

Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.

Recent findings suggest that according to the EKS documentation, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process on the parent instance releases a Firecracker microVM as a first-level guest with hardware-assisted virtualization, after which an agent inside the VM runs the pod’s containers through its own containerd and the two sides communicate over virtio and vsock. The result is a sandbox that shares neither kernel nor memory mappings with the parent instance or any other sandbox, while the containers themselves start unchanged. How the nodes get there depends on the cluster type: on EKS Auto Mode the two RuntimeClasses ship with every cluster and sandbox-capable nodes are provisioned on demand, whereas on standard EKS a team builds a sandbox-enabled AMI for its node groups or Karpenter.

(Source: Amazon EKS User Guide).

Sources indicate that what separates the two modes is which side of the boundary is trusted. Isolated mode trusts the parent instance and not the guest, which is why kubectl exec, logs, and process listing keep working, whereas confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted and moves enforcement inside the VM: a Cedar policy generated from the pod spec pins image digests, arguments, environment, mounts and capabilities, exec and stdin are denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures the image and policy into PCRs, and a KMS key policy can release secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match. Image layers can be encrypted as well, so the parent moves ciphertext it never reads.

That chain only holds if something checks the measurements, and the documentation claims so: without a KMS policy or external verifier checking the PCR values, "the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete." Separately from either mode, a network-isolated annotation boots the sandbox with no network device at all, which also removes DNS, NTP, IMDS and Pod Identity and breaks HTTP and TCP probes.

Industry observers note that sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero, read the documentation the same way and drew out what isolated mode leaves to the operator: the protection "only runs in one direction," so a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, writes the pod's /etc/hosts, and can mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node. He also lists prerequisites the blog post does not, among them Kubernetes 1.36 or later, a launch template with Nitro Enclaves enabled on managed node groups, without which "sandboxed pods sit in Pending," and Pod Identity rather than IRSA for credentials. On AWS's description of performance as near-native, he advises treating it "as a vendor claim" and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency.

Beyond agents, AWS lists multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs, and points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted VM in about two seconds.

Recent findings suggest that the constraints are on the considerations page, and the largest is GPU and device passthrough, which is not supported at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class. Density is capped twice over: total sandbox vCPUs may not exceed five times the node's vCPU count, and neither may the number of sandboxes, halved on CPU-overcommit types, which gives a 4-vCPU node room for twenty 1-vCPU sandboxes or five 4-vCPU ones. Simultaneous multithreading costs more than the arithmetic suggests, because core scheduling stops two sandboxes sharing the sibling threads of one core and leaves roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable; Graviton, with one thread per core, is unaffected.

In a recent development, the nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox, which has offered a gvisor RuntimeClass since 2019 and more recently a microvm class built on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor. gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel, starts in under 200 milliseconds and supports CUDA on a subset of GPUs; Google's microVM option carries a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod, starts in one to two seconds and does not support GPUs. AWS has taken the VM side of that split and expressed its overhead as density and threads rather than per-pod resources.

On EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker are supported natively and patches are available for other virtual machine monitors. The EC2 User Guide carries the supported instance list and notes that snapshot, restore and live migration are not available.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

Tech Report: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, and more.
