📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dr. Shaun Passley is Chairman and CEO of ZenaTech, bringing a background in enterprise software development and technology entrepreneurship to autonomous drone systems. He founded Epazz in 2000 and established ZenaTech in 2017, building on his software experience to connect aircraft, AI analytics, and business workflows. His work focuses on making drone technology practical for organizations that need better ways to collect data, automate fieldwork, and manage complex operations.

Recent findings suggest that zenaTech develops AI-powered drone, Drone as a Service, enterprise software, and quantum technology solutions. Through ZenaDrone and its service operations, the company combines aircraft design, data capture, and analytics for applications including surveying, inspections, agriculture, and warehouse inventory management. In this interview, Passley discusses autonomous navigation, the commercial model for drone services, and the technical and operational work required to bring coordinated drone fleets into everyday business workflows.

It has been revealed that you founded Epazz in 2000 and went on to establish ZenaTech in 2017, transitioning from enterprise software into AI-powered autonomous drones. What inspired this shift, and what opportunities did you identify that traditional drone manufacturers were overlooking?

According to recent reports, it started with a software test in Ireland. We were developing supply chain software for agriculture and brought a third-party drone to test it for plant identification. The drone was cumbersome to set up and struggled with the rugged terrain, constant rain, and changes in altitude. It didn’t have the sensors needed to adapt to those conditions, so we decided to build our own.

We also saw agriculture, especially spot spraying, was an obvious opportunity. There is a lot more that can be done with drones in data collection, pick harvesting, killing weeds and generally in improving yields. That’s the type of technology you will start to see commercialized heavily in the next three to five years. Much of that work is still labor-intensive. We saw an opportunity to build the hardware and software together and offer it as an accessible and cost-effective service.

Recent findings suggest that our background in enterprise software gave us an advantage. We understood the need and had the skills to connect drone hardware with software that could process data and automate workflows. As we began looking at industries like land surveying, infrastructure inspection, and warehouse logistics, we saw significant opportunities to modernize processes that still relied heavily on manual labor and outdated under digitized systems.

We also recognized early that collecting aerial data was only part of the solution. Businesses need technology that can process that information and turn it into actionable insights. That led us to developing and manufacturing our own drone hardware through ZenaDrone, integrated with AI analytics and enterprise software. We saw an opportunity to build an integrated platform and delivery mechanism that can automate entire workflows, rather than simply manufacture drones. This led to establishing our Drone as a Service business, currently a growing global brand, providing these turnkey, on-site services in a host of sectors.

Recent findings suggest that artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly central to drone technology. How does ZenaTech integrate AI and machine learning into its drone platforms, and what capabilities distinguish an AI-powered autonomous drone from a conventional drone operating on preprogrammed flight paths?

Traditional drones operating on preprogrammed flight paths follow a defined set of instructions. AI-powered autonomous drones can use onboard sensors, computer vision, and machine learning to interpret their surroundings and respond to changing conditions.

According to recent reports, take our IQ Nano indoor drone. With onboard computer vision and obstacle avoidance sensors, it’s designed to operate inside warehouses without GPS. It can navigate around obstacles, scan inventory barcodes, and upload data into inventory management systems. The broader opportunity is enabling drones to collect, interpret, and act on information with greater independence.

We are integrating AI into our drone platforms to support capabilities such as obstacle avoidance, autonomous navigation, predictive analytics, and automated backend data processing across our platform.

ZenaTech has embraced a Drone as a Service model to make autonomous drone technology more accessible. What are the biggest barriers preventing businesses from adopting AI-powered drones, and how does your Drone as a Service approach address challenges such as cost, technical expertise, and operational complexity?

It has been revealed that for most business customers, their focus isn’t on drone ownership. They care more about completing the job faster, safely, and at a competitive cost.

Sources indicate that the biggest barriers for businesses are the upfront investment, technical expertise, and operational requirements involved in managing commercial drone fleets. Organizations need to deal with trained pilots, recurring maintenance, regulatory compliance, and systems to process the data once it’s been collected.

Our Drone as a Service model addresses these challenges by providing turnkey drone-powered services on a subscription or usage basis. We manage the aircraft, pilots, compliance, data capture, and analytics. Customers get access to drone technology and its benefits automating the task without having to manage the operations themselves.

This makes it easier for businesses to adopt autonomous technology while focusing on the services and outcomes they need. It also allows us to introduce automation into industries that might struggle with the upfront cost or technical requirements.

It has been revealed that zenaTech recently reported 316% year-over-year revenue growth in Q2 2026, with DaaS accounting for the vast majority of revenue. How much of this growth reflects increasing customer demand for AI-powered automation, and what indicators do you use to measure the actual productivity improvements delivered to customers?

Recent findings suggest that acquisitions and then integrating our drones into the workflows for services such as surveys, mapping and inspections have been major drivers of ZenaTech growth. Our goal is to make the businesses we acquire more productive and create margin growth and leverage across our growing network of almost 45 global DaaS locations.

Sources indicate that our growth reflects a combination of strategic acquisitions, expanding demand for drone-powered services, and the operational efficiencies we’re introducing across our Drone as a Service network. In the second quarter of 2026, revenue increased 316% year over year, with Drone as a Service accounting for approximately 93% of total revenue. More recently, we reported average organic revenue growth of 27.1% across approximately 20 Drone as a Service locations acquired in 2025, with some locations growing by more than 40%.

Sources indicate that we measure productivity through practical outcomes: how quickly teams can complete fieldwork, how fast customers receive data, and how many additional projects existing teams can handle. Across our Drone as a Service operations, we survey more than 125 active projects per week. We have also reported internal estimates of delivering data 60% faster and reducing project costs by approximately half compared with traditional ground-based survey methods. Our priority is to increase operational capacity while improving efficiency and safety.

Acquisitions have become a major component of ZenaTech’s expansion strategy, particularly in surveying and engineering services. How do you integrate AI-powered drone technology into these established businesses, and what opportunities exist to automate workflows that have traditionally required significant manual labor?

We acquire established surveying, geospatial mapping and inspection businesses with experienced and licensed professionals, and existing revenue and customer base, then we introduce our drone technology to improve how they operate.

Recent findings suggest that regarding efficiency, in most cases, traditional surveys require crews to spend days collecting measurements often across challenging terrain. Drones equipped with photogrammetry and LiDAR capabilities can collect precise spatial data more efficiently and reduce the need for manual fieldwork. We also train licensed professionals, including surveyors and inspectors, to operate our autonomous systems. They already understand the work and have the expertise to do it well. All we do is give them better tools so they can get better results, faster and safer.

Beyond surveying, we’re expanding into services such as power washing for business exteriors and public infrastructure, inventory management for large warehouses, and construction progress monitoring for AI data centers and commercial building projects. We also offer end-to-end data management services to help customers access accurate site data more efficiently, streamline project workflows, and reduce project delays.

In a recent development, autonomous drones operating in complex environments must process large amounts of sensor and visual data while making decisions in real time. What are the most significant technical challenges involved in achieving reliable autonomy, and how is ZenaTech approaching areas such as computer vision, obstacle avoidance, and edge AI processing?

Sources indicate that one of our key priorities is advancing drones’ ability to accurately interpret their surroundings, process data in real time, and operate reliably across a wide range of dynamic environments. We’ve encountered this firsthand with our IQ Nano indoor drone. During an early warehouse pilot, dim lighting and reflective packaging made it difficult to accurately read inventory barcodes.

We addressed this challenge by training the AI vision system to recognize glare and distortion, analyze images from multiple angles, and identify the clearest image for barcode recognition.

We also developed an AI-enabled camera system with integrated LED illumination to improve data capture in low-light environments. Our drone platforms incorporate onboard AI, computer vision, and advanced sensors to support autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and real-time data collection and analysis. These capabilities are particularly notable in GPS-denied environments, where drones must navigate without relying on satellite positioning.

Sources indicate that another challenge is determining which decisions drones can safely make autonomously and when human intervention is needed. Drones can already follow programmed routes, while more advanced systems can adjust their paths as conditions change. Wider adoption depends on demonstrating that those decisions are reliable, remain within defined operating limits, and meet regulatory requirements. The FAA permits autonomous flight under Part 107, while requiring the remote pilot to retain the ability to direct the aircraft. The next step is to strengthen decision-making in unexpected situations while maintaining appropriate human oversight. Operators need confidence in both what the system can do and how it responds when something goes wrong.

Agriculture represents a significant opportunity for AI-powered drones, particularly in precision spraying, crop monitoring, and resource optimization. How are ZenaTech’s platforms evolving to support these applications, and how close are we to agricultural drones that can independently identify crop conditions and take corrective actions with minimal human intervention?

I think agriculture will become significantly more automated over the next three to five years.

It’s a significant opportunity for AI-powered drones, particularly as farmers and growers look for ways to reduce costs, optimize resources, and ultimately improve yields. At ZenaTech, we’re advancing precision agriculture solutions through our ZenaDrone platforms, which combine autonomous flight, advanced imaging, and AI analytics to support crop health monitoring, early detection of plant stress, and more targeted agricultural treatments.

In September, we announced the initial prototype and the start of the testing phase for our IQ Octo drone. This platform is specifically designed for precision agriculture imaging, AI analytics, and includes autonomous spraying and seeding. More recently, we started developing a mobile drone operations trailer to support automated, multi-drone on-site agricultural services. The mobile trailer enables drones to land and automatically recharge batteries, refill drone spray tanks with liquid agricultural inputs and replenish seed hoppers, reducing downtime between flights and operating with minimal human intervention. Our goal is to advance our development to bring these capabilities into agricultural workflows to help monitor crop conditions, support targeted treatments, and optimize manual labor requirements.

Sources indicate that zenaTech has unveiled research into quantum-enabled navigation systems designed to support drone operations in GPS-denied environments. What role do you envision quantum technologies playing alongside AI in autonomous navigation, and what technical milestones must be achieved before these capabilities become commercially practical?

Sources indicate that GPS signals can be jammed and spoofed, particularly in defense environments. We need drones that can navigate reliably when satellite positioning is not available.

We see quantum technologies as a complement to AI, combining quantum-based sensing with AI-driven path correction to enable more accurate navigation without relying on satellite signals.

At ZenaTech, we’ve advanced our quantum navigation system into the testing phase at our facility in Sharjah, UAE, starting with IQ Nano in GPS-denied environments. We plan to expand field testing to the ZenaDrone 1000 and other drone platforms. Our current focus is on validating accuracy and reliability under real-world conditions. Our long-term objective is to give autonomous drones another reliable way to navigate when satellite positioning fails.

These are important steps toward integrating quantum-enabled navigation into our broader autonomous drone portfolio for defense and commercial applications.

In a recent development, defense and government applications are becoming an increasingly crucial area of development for autonomous drone systems. How does ZenaTech approach the balance between AI-driven autonomy and human oversight, particularly in sensitive applications involving surveillance, threat detection, and autonomous decision-making?

AI-driven autonomy has the potential to improve situational awareness, operational efficiency, and safety in defense and government applications. However, I believe human operators must retain the ability to override an autonomous system. That means having a kill switch to stop or safely terminate the mission if something goes wrong.

Sources indicate that zenaTech is developing autonomous systems for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, cargo transport, and counter-UAS operations. Our integrated counter-UAS system is being designed to combine AI-powered threat detection and tracking with autonomous swarm coordination, allowing a single operator to oversee multiple interceptor drones. Our focus is on using AI to process information, support faster decision-making, and reduce personnel exposure to hazardous environments while developing systems that can operate reliably in complex defense settings.

Industry observers note that looking ahead over the next three to five years, how do you envision the convergence of AI, autonomous robotics, and enterprise software transforming the industries ZenaTech serves? You could have robots that automatically insert information into the company’s ERP solution, and the ERP solution could tell the robot to perform a certain number of tasks on some type of schedule set by a human being.

Industry observers note that when it comes to our drone platforms, we’re moving toward a future where autonomous drones become integrated into everyday business operations, managing complex workflows with less manual intervention. In a recent development, over the next three to five years, I’m expecting to see coordinated fleets of intelligent drones perform simultaneous and connected tasks, from collecting and analyzing data to supporting operational decisions in real time. Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model.
  • The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet.
  • Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

It has been revealed that in this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:.

Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:.

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

Industry observers note that I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The latest material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a major part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

It has been revealed that this project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

In that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Sources indicate that here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:.

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Recent findings suggest that those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:.

I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I rolled out the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

According to recent reports, fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

Disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

Recent findings suggest that the library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

It has been revealed that p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

His blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a big pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

In a recent development, the gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

In a recent development, the pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Recent findings suggest that here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

It has been revealed that the tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

No human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

According to recent reports, the interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

It has been revealed that if we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Sources indicate that before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:.

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

Industry observers note that with that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were launched for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:.

Recent findings suggest that the three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

In a recent development, the pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

According to recent reports, in every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

Sources indicate that this is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, indicates almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

It has been revealed that what the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

One more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

It has been revealed that the paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste indicates the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Recent findings suggest that surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

It has been revealed that to choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

In a recent development, since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

According to recent reports, failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

Sources indicate that I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs debuted with it have been running clean since.

According to recent reports, the reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

Sources indicate that the rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Sources indicate that smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

In a recent development, and the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

It has been revealed that and underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:.

In a recent development, the rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

The per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

According to recent reports, the method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christoph Hellwig has announced the initial public release of XRAID—declustered parity RAID that is integrated into XFS.

In a recent development, the two primary aims of XRAID are to support parity RAID on zoned devices like SMR hard drives, and to provide a fast RAID implementation without inherent data integrity problems. XRAID, just like zoned XFS also works on conventional hard drives and SSDs. Optimizing for SSD performance has not been a focus, but even without that, writes are up to 20 times faster than mdraid. [...].

Work on XRAID has been ongoing for a year and a half, and while we aren't anywhere near ready for an upstream submission, we are interested in feedback and testing from a wider audience now. The current implementation supports zero to 2 parities. We did experiments with the SnapRAID parity library to support 3 and more parities, and while that is not included in the current version, support for more parities is planned and the code is prepared for it.

The xfsprogs branch includes mkfs support and a newly introduced "xraid" utility for managing devices and inspecting an XRAID file-systems. We have also extended Zonar (The zoned file-system visualisation tool) to show how each logical zone maps onto physical zones on devices.

Hellwig gave a presentation at FOSSY in August on this topic; video of the talk does not seem to be available yet, but his slides are available.

CNBC reported on November 16, 2026, that Altimeter Capital looks to invest $5 billion in Anthropic’s proposed initial public offering, after founder and CEO Brad Gerstner disclosed the plan on “Halftime Report.” The planned investment is five times the largest amount he had previously committed to an IPO.

“I think this is a cornerstone compounder for a long time,” Gerstner said. He attributed the size of Altimeter’s planned order to Anthropic’s presentation of the business and its financial position, and said he remained optimistic despite a semiconductor downturn and an anti-AI swing in Washington.

Altimeter is a technology-focused investment firm managing funds across public and private markets, with a stated aim of serving as a long-term partner to companies entering public markets. The planned order would extend an existing relationship. Anthropic’s May 28, 2026 Series H announcement named Altimeter among the lead investors in a $65 billion round that valued the tech giant at $965 billion post-money.

Anthropic’s preliminary IPO terms, filed November 10, 2026, cover 825 million Class A shares at an estimated $70 to $78 each: approximately 801.4 million from the manufacturer and 23.6 million from selling stockholders, whose sales will not generate proceeds for Anthropic. The company has applied to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under ANT, and the CNBC report put the expected valuation at about $1.4 trillion. Altimeter’s proposed order is separate from a $26 billion Class N private placement by Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners. That contingent placement uses the IPO price and is scheduled to close immediately after the offering; its shares are not registered in the Class A offering.

Sources indicate that anthropic’s IPO materials identified November 18, 2026 as the expected pricing date and November 19, 2026 as the expected start of public trading, subject to regulatory clearance, investor demand and market conditions. They also state that no investor is guaranteed all or any requested shares, so Gerstner’s announcement describes an intended order rather than a confirmed allocation.

Anthropic reported $17.0 billion of revenue for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up 1,127% from a year earlier. The revenue figure supports the growth component of Gerstner’s thesis; the offering documents show a more complicated picture on profitability and capital needs.

It has been revealed that the IPO materials reported a 15% adjusted operating margin, which excludes stock-based compensation, non-cash charitable contributions and a legal settlement, alongside a negative 3% operating margin under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). Anthropic’s $23.3 billion quarterly net loss included a $21.9 billion non-cash charge related to changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs as its valuation increased.

Industry observers note that the amended registration statement disclosed approximately $900.9 billion of aggregate committed spending entered into as of or after September 30, 2026, substantially all for compute and infrastructure. Approximately $451.6 billion is expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030. The commitments include purchase agreements and leases, including leases not yet commenced, making them a central measure of the capital behind Anthropic’s expansion prepares.

In a recent development, the central tension for the listing is therefore between rapid adoption and positive adjusted operating performance on one side, and GAAP losses and substantial infrastructure commitments on the other. Gerstner’s planned order backs the long-term business case, but the scale of those commitments makes execution and continued access to capital central to Anthropic’s public-market transition.

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • According to recent reports, earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each upcoming agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

In a recent development, funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

Industry observers note that recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:.

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

In a recent development, or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

It has been revealed that funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

Sources indicate that A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent notes so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

It has been revealed that compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

In a recent development, the lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

According to recent reports, your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

According to recent reports, funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Sources indicate that ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

It has been revealed that for comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

Sources indicate that longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Open-Sources Emulator for Local Testing of 200+ Services by Coding Agents.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

Recent findings suggest that AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services. AWS Emulator lets developers and coding agents create resources, hit the same errors AWS would return, and iterate without provisioning cloud resources or incurring service charges for the operations it emulates.

According to recent reports, teams point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at it with environment variables such as AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, leaving application code unchanged. On Linux it installs as an RPM or Debian package for x86_64 or aarch64; on macOS and Windows, AWS documents a short Dockerfile and does not publish a prebuilt image. Rust tests can use an embedded mode that runs the emulator inside the test process and wires its HTTP client into the AWS SDK for Rust. An aws-emulator skill can start the emulator for coding agents and check a project against published fidelity tests. Written in Rust, it is generated from more than 400 Smithy API models AWS publishes for the SDKs, according to Swaminathan Sivasubramanian.

AWS says agents wrote and tested the code. Matthew Goldberg, a senior principal engineer at AWS, describes three teams: one writes fidelity tests from the public API models and verifies them against real AWS, one replays those tests and files problems, and one implements each fix. Every change must pass a merge gate that checks compilation, coding standards, security, and fidelity regressions. The work runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit.

How closely the emulator matches AWS varies by service. AWS publishes versioned fidelity tests and per-service scores with each release; a test passes only when every call matches AWS, including status codes, side effects, and exact errors. Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 with the error code NotImplemented. AWS states fidelity is closest on control-plane APIs, while data-plane behavior and support for CloudFormation, Terraform, and the AWS CDK vary by service. Documented limits include no evaluation of IAM or resource-based policies, so it must not be used to test security; a single shared account and Region per process; in-memory state that disappears when the process stops; and no testing for long-running use or load. The evaluation suite includes tests the emulator does not yet pass.

Developers already have several local AWS stand-ins, including LocalStack, Floci, and moto. AWS Emulator is generated from AWS's own API models, ships official fidelity scores, and is dedicated to the public domain, but it is not a drop-in replacement for every workflow those tools cover, especially permission testing and infrastructure-as-code pipelines.

According to recent reports, AWS just released a free local emulator of its APIs, made for coding agents and written entirely by agents. I counted its published fidelity tests: S3, DynamoDB and SQS pass about 2 in 3. CloudFormation passes under 1 in 5.

Yurii Serhiichuk compared it with existing emulators and published a container image and GitHub Action to cover a packaging gap:.

It has been revealed that AWS shipped AWS Emulator today - think LocalStack/Floci but native. Rust, built by agents (so hopefully it gets updated pretty fast). No public docker image though, and no GitHub action. So I filled that part.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Emulator is generally available at no additional service fee. Source is on GitHub under the CC0 1.0 Universal public domain dedication, except third-party code in the vendor/ directory, which is under the Apache License 2.0. Setup details are in the user guide, and fidelity scores ship with each release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

In a recent development, IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Sources indicate that the full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:.

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

It has been revealed that after GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

Sources indicate that the gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it reveals that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • LangSmith formerly organized incoming traces by project, without a durable connection to the agent that generated them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LangChain on November 16, 2026 detailed a rebuild of LangSmith that gives every registered AI agent a persistent record with a named owner, globally unique immutable ID and type, connecting deployment, tracing, evaluation and governance across runtimes.

LangSmith formerly organized incoming traces by project, without a durable connection to the agent that generated them. Separate environments also produced unlinked pools of telemetry even when they belonged to the same agent. Local, development, staging and production environments now sit beneath one agent ID, with their traces and lifecycle tools attached to the same record.

Sources indicate that the redesign is intended to reduce context switching for engineers moving among tracing, monitoring and deployment tools. It also gives platform teams a consistent way to answer ownership, cost and performance questions. Opening an agent record provides one-click access to its traces, evaluations, Agent Server and issues surfaced by Engine.

It has been revealed that the architecture expands on the LangSmith Agent Platform introduced in LangChain’s November 13, 2026 Series C announcement, which presented runtime, improvement and governance as three pillars. The upcoming post supplies the data model joining those functions to individual agents.

Type determines what appears on an agent’s dashboard, which data connections it supports and how it is evaluated. General-purpose and coding agent types are available, while LangChain lists voice as forthcoming. The planned voice type reflects requirements such as low latency and audio quality in addition to solving a customer’s problem.

LangChain’s examples contrast the initial dashboards. A general-purpose view combines an agent’s description, recent activity, online monitoring, commonly used models and tools, and failures identified by Engine. A coding view instead emphasizes merged pull requests, token cost and categories of completed work; it can also connect to a GitHub repository to track downstream outcomes.

Assigning a type activates a preconfigured dashboard without requiring a team to construct custom views. Because every agent of a given type is measured on the same basis, results can be compared across teams working on similar agents.

LangSmith can register agents running on external platforms that support OpenTelemetry Protocol, alongside agents built internally. Registered agents are measured the same way without requiring every team to adopt one runtime. Cost and quality metrics roll up across environments, and the named owner plus detailed traces provide a starting point for investigating a cost spike or performance change.

Sources indicate that the platform remains composable. An agent can stay on its existing runtime and use LangSmith’s tracing, evaluation, dataset, annotation and Engine tools once it sends traces to the platform. The agent registry and LLM Gateway add organization-level visibility and controls for registered agents. Teams can instead describe an agent in Studio’s natural-language builder, write code with LangChain’s open-source harnesses or another framework, and deploy on Agent Server.

It has been revealed that for customers using both Engine and Agent Server, one integration lets Engine test a proposed fix against a preview deployment before the change is merged into production. That connects diagnosis and verification to the same agent record rather than leaving them in separate workflows.

At publication, the rebuilt LangSmith was available globally in cloud, bring-your-own-cloud and self-hosted environments. Centralized dashboards operate at workspace level. LangChain’s roadmap adds organization-level views that aggregate performance and trends across a organization, plus identity-provider registration so security teams can manage and audit agents alongside other organizational identities.

Sources indicate that langChain is also connecting existing capabilities (including Engine red-teaming, custom annotation apps, evaluation datasets, trajectory collection and fine-tuning) around the shared record. Its proposed workflow would send reviewed production examples into evaluation datasets and turn trajectories from successful runs into fine-tuning data. Those connections are part of the roadmap; the individual components already exist.

In a recent development, for enterprises managing internally built, vendor-supplied and employee-adopted agents, the rebuild establishes ownership and consistent evaluation as common controls across a mixed fleet. The cross-runtime registry is available, but the broader oversight layer—manufacturer-wide dashboards and identity-provider management—remains unfinished.

NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

In a recent development, neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

According to recent reports, multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Industry observers note that pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

Recent findings suggest that to get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

In a recent development, one NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Recent findings suggest that late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding fresh documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

Sources indicate that so we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

Sources indicate that we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Sources indicate that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

Industry observers note that neoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Olimpiu Pop: OpenSSF is definitely a stronghold for security. Before the recent surge in AI, there was a strong push to move security to the left—getting tools and practices closer to development teams. Historically, security was often left for the end alongside documentation and other crucial tasks.

In my experience, whenever something bad happened, the security architect had to scramble down, fix it, and then try to convince developers to adopt the fix. As we record this in early November, we've seen widespread scrambling over PyPI incidents and others, as security incidents continue to rise.
