📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility.

Nov 16, 2026 18 min read.

Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.

Sources indicate that application logs, infrastructure metrics, API telemetry, security events, job failures, service-management tickets, and business alerts all describe pieces of the same operating environment. The hard problem is not collecting another signal. It is connecting those signals rapidly enough to understand what is happening, what it may affect, and what should happen next.

Agentic AI is attractive because it can reason across that fragmented evidence, retrieve operational knowledge, call tools, and coordinate multi-step work. But a utility organization cannot treat an agent the same way it treats a conversational assistant. A wrong summary is inconvenient. A wrong production action can affect a customer-facing service, a safety-related workflow, regulatory reporting, or a system that participates in reliable energy delivery.

It has been revealed that microsoft Ignite 2026; Explore What's Next in AI and Software Engineering - Learn how to architect agentic systems, modernize cloud infrastructure, and tackle emerging engineering challenges. Get practical insights from Microsoft experts and industry leaders. Microsoft Ignite is less than two weeks away! Register now to join us in person or attend online for free, November 17–20.

This article describes the architecture pattern we used for an agentic operations platform in a regulated utility environment. The reference implementation uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, retrieval over enterprise runbooks and incident history, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces.

It has been revealed that the model can propose anything. It can execute only what the policy gate authorizes, through the governed tool path, with human approval wherever policy requires it. Authority never lives inside the model.

It has been revealed that some capabilities, especially prediction and autonomous remediation, are intentionally enabled incrementally rather than all at once. That is not a limitation to hide. In a regulated environment, the ability to expand autonomy gradually and revoke it quickly is part of the architecture.

In a recent development, A large utility estate spans custom applications, SaaS products, cloud platforms, integration layers, databases, observability tools, field and operational systems, and third-party services. Each domain can be monitored well in isolation while the end-to-end service remains difficult to reason about.

In a recent development, the recurring operational gaps are familiar. Related signals appear in separate tools and are correlated manually. Technical severity is visible, but the business consequence is not. Runbooks and lessons learned exist, but they are spread across wikis, ticket histories, shared drives, and the memory of experienced engineers. Thresholds tell teams when a known condition has already occurred; weaker precursors across dependent systems are easy to miss. When action is finally taken, the evidence tying the change to its rationale, authorization, approver, and outcome may be assembled after the fact.

Industry observers note that this is especially vital in utilities because the governing context is not uniform. Regulatory requirements vary across utility sectors, operational environments, and jurisdictions. For example, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) requirements apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) and defined in-scope BES Cyber Systems. At the same time, customer-facing services, billing, field operations, and other utility programs may be subject to applicable industry-specific, federal, state, or local regulatory requirements.

The architecture therefore has to do more than produce a better dashboard. It must correlate across domains, reason with trusted operational knowledge, map technical events to business impact, support prediction without pretending prediction is certain, and preserve an execution model that security, compliance, operators, and auditors can understand.

Figure 1. Fragmented observability leaves operations teams to correlate application, infrastructure, integration, security, and service-management signals manually (Image source: created by the author).

Recent findings suggest that the organizing idea is an AI control plane. The term is borrowed deliberately from networking and cloud infrastructure, where the control plane decides what should happen and a separate plane carries it out. The separation is useful here for the same reasons: safety, auditability, and blast-radius containment.

It has been revealed that figure 2. The AI control plane separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The model can propose broadly; only policy-authorized actions can cross into the execution plane. (Image source: created by the author).

In the reasoning plane, the orchestrator and domain agents can analyze events, retrieve context, compare an incident with historical patterns, estimate business impact, predict likely failure modes, and propose remediation. None of those components holds authority to change a production system directly.

A proposed action crosses into the execution plane only through a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway. The gate decides whether the action is permitted and what approval is required. The gateway enforces the final authorization, obtains narrowly scoped credentials, invokes the target system, records the result, and performs or requests post-action validation.

This distinction matters when the model is wrong. A hallucinated root cause in a conventional autonomous design can become a bad action. In this design, it becomes a bad proposal. Policy can reject the proposal, a human can review it, or the gateway can deny authorization. The model’s error still matters, but its cost is limited by construction.

Sources indicate that the reference implementation runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore supplies managed agent runtime, memory, gateway, identity, and observability integrations with Amazon Bedrock for model access and Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval over enterprise knowledge. AgentCore Policy, generally available since March 2026, covers the boundary this pattern relies on: rules authored in natural language or policy-as-code are compiled to Cedar, AWS’s open-source authorization policy language, and attached to an AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates every agent-tool request before allowing or denying it. That is deterministic, action-level authorization enforced at the gateway rather than inside agent logic, and teams starting today should evaluate it before building an equivalent. In this design, AgentCore Gateway is the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. AgentCore Evaluations supports continuous and on-demand evaluation of agent behavior.

MCP is used at the tool boundary to standardize how tools are described and invoked. A schema-defined tool boundary gives the platform one place to constrain operations, validate arguments, enforce policy, and record evidence.

According to recent reports, the "one place" property is key. A tool gateway is only a governance boundary if agents cannot bypass it. In our design, that means no target-system credentials in the reasoning runtime, deny-by-default identity policies, tightly restricted network paths, and credentials exposed only to the tool implementation that needs them. The principle is simple: one door to production, with every control attached to that door.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. The pattern mapped onto AWS services. Everything in the reasoning plane can only propose; requests cross the dashed boundary solely through the policy gate and AgentCore Gateway, the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. (Image source: created by the author).

It has been revealed that the pattern is not tied to AWS. It needs a managed agent runtime, a retrieval layer, and a policy-enforcing tool gateway that agents cannot bypass. On Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the runtime, Microsoft Entra supplies agent identities, and Azure AI Search handles retrieval, with Azure API Management serving as the tool gateway and an AI gateway for model and MCP traffic (some of these governance features are still in preview). On Google Cloud, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides Agent Runtime and Agent Identity, with Agent Gateway as the tool gateway, enforcing IAM access policies and Model Armor screening for prompt injection.

The boundary that matters sits between the agentic layer and the tool gateway; everything above it reasons, and nothing above it can act.

Recent findings suggest that table 1. End-to-end responsibilities across the governed pipeline, from signal ingestion to the operations view.

The reasoning plane uses a hierarchical multi-agent structure rather than one large agent with broad access. A narrow agent with a bounded responsibility is easier to test, constrain, evaluate, and explain than a monolithic agent that knows every domain and can call every tool.

It has been revealed that the Orchestrator Agent is the entry point for normalized operational events. It determines the analysis required, routes work to the appropriate domain agents, and assembles their findings. It coordinates but does not execute.

In a recent development, the Application Reliability Agent analyzes application failures and degradations against known patterns and recent history. The Platform Intelligence Agent looks at API and interface failures, latency, partial degradation, and upstream/downstream dependencies. The Business Impact Agent translates technical state into business consequences — for example, a risk to customer service, billing, a safety-related program, a reliability commitment, or a reporting deadline. The Remediation Agent is the only reasoning component allowed to propose a production-touching action, and its proposal still has no authority until it passes the policy and approval path.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4. The orchestrator decomposes each event and routes analysis to bounded domain agents; only the Remediation Agent proposes production actions, and those proposals still pass through policy and the tool gateway (Image source: created by the author).

Sources indicate that all agents use shared operational context retrieved from enterprise knowledge. The useful corpus is the organization’s runbooks, SOPs, architecture documentation, incident history, business rules, dependency maps, and known recovery procedures. Grounding a recommendation in the documented procedure for this environment produces a very different artifact from a plausible answer based only on general model training.

The quality of this layer depends heavily on knowledge hygiene. If a runbook is outdated, contradictory, or missing a rollback step, RAG will faithfully retrieve an outdated, contradictory, or incomplete instruction. Curation, ownership, versioning, and source traceability are therefore part of the operational design, not a content-management side project.

Sources indicate that in practice, every runbook carries a named owner and a last-review date, and retrieval returns both with each passage. Runbooks past their review interval are flagged to the owner, and operator rejections citing a faulty runbook are routed to the runbook’s owner for correction.

A common event contract is just as vital as the knowledge base. We normalize incoming signals into a small operational schema that includes the affected service or component, environment, event type, timestamp, source, technical severity, dependency identifiers, correlation keys, business-service mapping, and a reference back to the original evidence. The raw payload is preserved, but deterministic parsing and source adapters, not the LLM, establish basic facts such as which system emitted the event and whether two identifiers refer to the same service. A model can help interpret an unfamiliar log message, but those foundational facts are too important to leave to probabilistic extraction.

According to recent reports, the simplified example below shows a normalized event from the walkthrough scenario. The business-service mapping is looked up from the service catalog, not inferred by the model.

Consider a common integration-operations pattern. An API has not failed, but its latency begins to rise. At roughly the same time, a downstream integration starts retrying more frequently, and a processing queue grows. Each signal on its own may still be below a page-worthy threshold. Together they suggest that a customer-facing workflow could degrade if the pattern continues.

Recent findings suggest that the ingestion layer normalizes the three signals and preserves their source evidence. The orchestrator recognizes that the affected components share a dependency chain and asks the Platform Intelligence Agent to analyze the interface behavior. The Application Reliability Agent checks whether the application has shown a similar resource or connection pattern in prior incidents. The Business Impact Agent maps the dependency to the business service that relies on it.

Retrieval then pulls the current runbook for this failure class and the most relevant historical incidents. The agents don't merely summarize alerts; they produce a structured operational hypothesis: the likely failure mode, supporting evidence, dependent services that may be affected, and documented remediation options. If the evidence is weak or contradictory, that uncertainty is carried forward rather than hidden.

In a recent development, suppose the runbook permits two next steps: gather additional diagnostics and, if a specific condition is confirmed, restart a stateless component. The action catalog may classify the diagnostic tool as low risk and allow it to run automatically. In this deployment, the catalog maps the restart to a human-approval rule. The Remediation Agent can propose it, but it cannot decide to downgrade its risk because the model is confident.

In a recent development, when an operator approves the restart, the tool gateway verifies the approval reference and policy, obtains the scoped execution identity, invokes only the permitted operation, and captures the response. The workflow then checks the signals that motivated the action: latency, retry behavior, queue trend, and service health. If those conditions do not recover, the workflow does not mark the remediation successful simply because the restart command completed.

The architecture removes manual correlation and runbook hunting from a familiar operational problem while preserving the same controls an experienced engineer would expect before touching production.

Prediction is where the platform moves beyond faster incident summarization. The goal is to identify combinations of weak signals that historically precede a failure: rising latency, queue growth, retry behavior, resource saturation, repeated warning patterns, or anomalies that become meaningful only when correlated across a dependency chain.

The prediction layer can use historical incidents, time-series trends, dependency information, and semantic analysis of unstructured logs to produce a forward-looking statement: what may fail, on what horizon, through which mechanism, with what confidence, and with what likely business consequence.

The crucial design decision is what prediction is not allowed to do. A confidence score is not an authorization token. Predictions enter the same governed path as observed incidents. They carry evidence, confidence, and business-weighted risk so operators can decide how to respond.

False positives are expected. They should be measured, reviewed, and reduced over time. Overselling prediction is one of the fastest ways to lose operator trust.

It has been revealed that human control should not be a sentence in a governance document. It should sit directly on the execution path.

Sources indicate that the platform maps every candidate action to a predefined risk class outside the model. An approved action catalog drives that classification, not the model deciding whether its own proposal is dangerous. The catalog can consider the operation, target environment, blast radius, reversibility, data impact, and dependency sensitivity, but the resulting policy is fixed, versioned, testable, and reviewable.

Table 2. Action risk classification and governance requirements.

This is intentionally conservative. In the early stages of deployment, even some low-risk actions may remain approval-only until the team has enough evidence to allow automatic execution.

The policy record should be concrete enough to test without an LLM. For each permitted operation, we keep the tool identifier, target environment, allowed scope, risk class, required approval type, execution timeout, key preconditions, and expected postconditions, plus a link to the rollback procedure where rollback is meaningful. The agent may supply parameters such as a service name or requested capacity, but policy decides whether they fall inside the authorized envelope. The risk-driving facts should come from controlled configuration, inventory, or independently verified context, because asking the model to label its own proposal low, medium, or high leaves the authority decision with the model.

Sources indicate that figure 5. Deterministic policy maps each proposed action to a risk class and approval requirement before the governed tool gateway can execute it (Image source: created by the author).

Post-action validation is easy to underestimate. "API returned 200" is not the same as "the system is healthy," so a remediation workflow should validate the outcome it was meant to produce and escalate if the expected state is not restored.

In a recent development, the gateway also provides defense in depth. It scopes least-privilege credentials to specific tools, authorizes each agent-and-action combination independently, and rechecks required approvals at execution time instead of trusting an upstream component’s claim that they happened. It also validates tool arguments against their schemas. Every invocation records the requesting identity, policy decision, approval reference, inputs, result, and post-action health status.

Typed tools constrain what a manipulated agent can request, but they do not make prompt injection disappear, because an agent can still misuse an operation within its allowed scope. The control therefore comes from layers: treating ingested content as untrusted data, narrow tools, argument validation, least privilege, policy enforcement, approval requirements, network constraints, and post-action validation.

Content inspection adds one more layer at the same boundary; since June 2026, AgentCore Policy can evaluate Bedrock Guardrails to screen tool gateway inputs and outputs for prompt injection and sensitive-data exposure (initially in a subset of AWS Regions). Treat that as one more control on the door rather than a solution to injection, and keep the bounded-authority layers regardless of how good the detection gets.

For regulated operations, governance is not a section added after the architecture. It is why the architecture has this shape.

Industry observers note that teams should manage model and agent changes with the same discipline as other production software: version-controlled prompts and agent definitions, reviewed changes, evaluation before promotion, and rollback capability. Historical incidents and adversarial cases provide useful regression tests. Teams should sample production traces and evaluate them for task completion, tool selection, groundedness, safety, and policy adherence. They should also monitor confidence and recommendation quality for drift after deployment.

According to recent reports, teams should also minimize operational data. Logs and tickets can contain customer, employee, or security-sensitive information irrelevant to the reasoning task. Before broad ingestion, teams should establish data classification, domain isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, and retention rules. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications identifies prompt injection and excessive agency as distinct risks, and its agentic security guidance extends that thinking to goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and multi-agent interactions.

Audit evidence should answer more than "what did the system do?" For every consequential action, the organization should be able to reconstruct the originating signal, retrieved evidence, recommendation, applicable policy, human decision if required, executed operation, identity used, and validated result. Whether you can call that record immutable depends on the actual storage control; at minimum, it should be durable, access-controlled, tamper-evident, or otherwise protected according to enterprise evidence requirements.

In a recent development, the compliance mapping must be equally precise. NERC CIP does not apply to every application operated by an electric utility. For in-scope BES Cyber Systems, CIP-010-4 addresses configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-004-7 includes personnel and access-management requirements; CIP-011-3 addresses protection of BES Cyber System Information; and CIP-008-6 covers cyber-security incident reporting and response planning. An agentic platform can support the evidence needed for applicable requirements, but the platform itself does not create compliance.

Industry observers note that for customer-facing and regulated programs, evidence and reporting obligations may vary based on applicable jurisdictional requirements. Corporate applications outside CIP scope may instead fall under internal change controls, privacy requirements, or financial controls. The practical rule is to map evidence to the regime governing the specific system rather than labeling the entire utility estate "CIP compliant".

Frameworks such as NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can organize the broader AI governance program, but they complement rather than replace industry-specific requirements.

In regulated environments, organizations should measure agentic AI value against operational baselines, not unsupported improvement percentages. The signals we tracked included detection time from the earliest useful signal to an actionable alert; response time to validated resolution; prediction precision, false-positive rate, lead time, and operator-rated usefulness; engineering effort spent on manual correlation, after-hours paging, and repeated analysis; and governance measures such as approval latency, policy denials, blocked unauthorized actions, evidence completeness, and audit reconstruction time.

It has been revealed that we expanded autonomy in phases, one action class at a time. No action class moved forward on model confidence alone. Each step required agreement from the system owner and change-management reviewers, based on the evidence below.

It has been revealed that table 3. Phased autonomy progression and evidence requirements.

Recent findings suggest that agentic AI can correlate operational signals, assess business impact, and recommend remediation, but in mission-critical environments its value depends on how well its authority is governed. For teams adopting this pattern, a few recommendations stand out:.

The goal is not maximum autonomy, but evidence-based autonomy that can be safely governed and revoked.

Tech Report: tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • Industry observers note that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

Industry observers note that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

In a recent development, this work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Sources indicate that before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

Recent findings suggest that v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

In a recent development, the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

It has been revealed that the tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

In a recent development, each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

It has been revealed that BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

It has been revealed that real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Industry observers note that naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Fresh words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Recent findings suggest that caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

Recent findings suggest that the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Sources indicate that each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

It has been revealed that repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the latest merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

In a recent development, A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Sources indicate that training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we blueprint to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

In a recent development, will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As AI accelerates change across the enterprise, PwC's James Shira explains why security teams must rethink their approach to risk and adapt their strategies.
  • James Shira, global CISO and CIO of PwC, has spent more than two decades navigating the evolution of cybersecurity, from its early days as a largely technical function to its continuously growing role in corporate agendas and spending.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As AI accelerates change across the enterprise, PwC's James Shira explains why security teams must rethink their approach to risk and adapt their strategies.

James Shira, global CISO and CIO of PwC, has spent more than two decades navigating the evolution of cybersecurity, from its early days as a largely technical function to its continuously growing role in corporate agendas and spending. Shira's path into the industry was, as he puts it, as "consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow." Originally considering a career in law, Shira decided to pivot, more seriously considering pursuing cybersecurity through independent study, and then formal education. Today, he oversees both technology and security at one of the world's largest professional services firms, giving him a broad perspective on the challenges facing security leaders.

According to recent reports, in this episode of Heard It From a CISO with Dark Reading associate editor Kristina Beek, Shira discusses the skills and experience needed to build a career in cybersecurity, including the value of industry certifications, higher education, and on-the-job experience. He also examines the qualities that distinguish effective security teams, the challenges of balancing the CISO and CIO roles, and how security leaders can establish credibility with corporate boards. For Shira, successful leadership comes down to more than technical expertise. It involves building trust, communicating complex concerns clearly, and creating an environment where employees can develop.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls.

Shira also shares his thoughts on the topic on everyone's minds: artificial intelligence. He warns that rapid adoption is expanding attack surfaces, adding pressure on security teams, but also notes that AI technology will add opportunities for professionals seeking roles in the field. As for what's ahead, Shira expects significant societal and industry change and shares that this rate of change is likely to be the newly introduced standard — it’s best if everyone is prepared to go along for the ride.

This is part of Dark Reading's ongoing Heard It From a CISO video series, which features frank, exclusive conversations with cybersecurity leaders in the trenches. Check out the entire series here.

The way I describe it to our folks is that I talk about the concepts of internal equity and external equity. Your internal equity when you come out of college is zero. You're new; you're coming into the industry. You build that up over time with your employer. Obviously, you want to pick the right place to work, as best you can. Then, after five to seven years of experience, they make a choice about whether they're going to pursue a management track or a higher-end technical director or subject-matter-expert track.

Industry observers note that on your question about a four-year education versus certifications, my personal view is that if you want to be in a role similar to mine, or the same as mine, you're going to want that four-year degree. You may even want a master's eventually. If that's your intended path, I would encourage you, notwithstanding the loans, to complete your undergraduate degree. There are a lot of great schools with programs that can be helpful. If you look at that and say to yourself, "That's a significant debt burden, and I don't think it makes sense. Industry observers note that DR's Kristina Beek: That's a great insight. What interested me about PwC at that time was that it was a 160-plus-year-old institution. I had never worked in professional services; I had only worked in financial services. So a different industry interested me.

Industry observers note that I think the organization's values here at PwC were very consistent with mine, and it's been a privilege to be here. It sounds clichéd, but it's really a great place. The quality of people, on average, in my experience, has been really high. People have a desire to do the right thing, and as a CISO, that's incredibly helpful. A lot of our security strategy is culturally centered on employee behavior and training, so those things were very consistent and have been very helpful.

I know some CISOs drive programs through cultures that are less amenable. This culture was incredibly amenable to moving its security program to the next level. DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to a follow-up question. When it comes to a team, whether it's business-oriented or security-focused, what makes a great team? What kinds of people are you looking for, whether in terms of personality or skills?

Sources indicate that james Shira: I'm going to answer your question in reverse order. The people I like to work with don't come in a common package. I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times, but I think that makes for better decisions.

Recent findings suggest that the people I'm looking for don't have to have gone to a specific school. They don't necessarily need a traditional profile, but they definitely need to be self-confident and self-directed. I talk to the team a lot about emotional resiliency. I think it's a really important concept in the security industry because, when I got started, security was past the mailroom, past the bathrooms, in the basement somewhere, and rarely in the boardroom. Now, people coming into the field wouldn't even recognize that, because security is such a central, strategically critical issue for companies. I need that confidence in our employees so that, when they become the leaders they can be, they can flourish based on that confidence. It's hard to build a great team without that.

Recent findings suggest that the second piece I think is incredibly crucial is transparency. It's uncomfortable at times, and it can be challenging to answer the questions you get, but I think it provokes the kind of cultural engagement that makes for a great team.

The one thing I'll say lastly is that I don't think mediocrity, as a rule, fits in high-performing teams. You have to embrace your high performers, try to elevate and promote them, and create an environment where they can be as self-directed and successful as they can be.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. When you were answering that, one of the things you talked about was how the CISO role and cybersecurity in general are now in the boardroom. I see a lot of articles about how to communicate with C-suite members as a CISO, how to deal with friction, and how to get your board to believe you. What would you say about communicating your needs as a CISO to the rest of the board? Do you encounter friction in your experience, and how do you deal with that?

James Shira: I think it's a great question. I'm going to offer a point of view. I'll start by saying I've gotten it wrong. I don't have all the answers, but I've learned through mistakes and by having great mentors.

Industry observers note that I think credibility with a board starts, frankly, through delivery. The first thing you have to do is build a track record as best you can. That might sound counterintuitive: Don't I need the board's buy-in before I deliver? Somewhat, but I think conversations with our various boards here, and the conversations I've had previously, show that over time, through delivery of the program and driving the change you're advocating for, you can build a lot of credibility.

Recent findings suggest that the second of my three points is that you have to find your own authentic voice. Personally, I'm not a natural. I kind of joke with the team at times that I'm a radio guy, not a TV guy, and I've had to work at being a TV guy. You have to find your own authenticity through your own style. A lot of times, those of us who get the privilege of being in these C-level jobs receive a lot of advice and pressure about how to present and who to be. I would encourage people listening to find their own style and approach that works best for them. Obviously, measure it against how effective it is, but embrace the style that's authentic to you. For me, I just try to be myself with our board.

Industry observers note that the last thing I'd say, and I think it's maybe the most vital point, is that you have to bring the expertise to the board, not try to drag the board to your expertise. In our domain, don't underestimate how intimidating it can be for the people listening. It's security. They see the headlines. Maybe an concern has occurred in that business. As board members, they feel responsible for providing oversight over management, and they're under tremendous pressure to do so. Don't underestimate that.

If you come at them with a high degree of expertise, terms, acronyms, and things they don't understand, I've found that doesn't work. That would be one of the mistakes I've made in the past. What's worked well for me is not to dumb it down, but to simplify it. If you have enough mastery of a topic, you can describe it in a way that doesn't make the other person feel intimidated and helps them say, "OK, I get that." DR's Kristina Beek: While you're obviously CISO, you're also CIO, so you have two perspectives. What is it like balancing the responsibilities of both roles?

Sources indicate that james Shira: The good news is that, over the last eight years I've had the privilege of being in these roles, there's been a tremendous amount of harmonization between the technology transformation of large enterprises and the need to get the cyber piece right. Therefore, unlike when I started, when security was past the mailroom and in the basement, it's now such a primary issue for organizations that it's really on the CIO's agenda. I think having both of those skill sets is a very critical thing in this day and age.

The one difference I'd acknowledge for the audience, because otherwise anybody watching would think I missed it, is that at times the CIO role can be inherently more political than the CISO role. Let me explain briefly. As a CISO, you objectively know what good looks like: Don't have a breach, don't have an incident, improve your audit posture, drive good risk management, and so on. What good looks like in the CIO world can sometimes be less black and white and more gray. It can change in a way that a traditional CISO might find challenging to navigate.

There are differences, but in summary, it's a very complementary experience for me. The biggest challenge is time management and moving time between the different things.

Recent findings suggest that DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. AI is, of course, always part of the conversation. It's changing how attackers work, and it's also changing how organizations operate. What do you see as the biggest cybersecurity opportunity or risk associated with AI right now?

James Shira: I think the most vital problem with AI, straight down the middle, is how it changes, evolves, and increases an organization's attack surface. The second issue is the rate of change it brings: how fast it moves and how fast systems have to move. Those are the two dynamics.

In a recent development, what happens to the size of your attack surface? AI can really explode it. At the same time, AI puts pressure on the pace of change across the whole security function. For us specifically, that means dealing with the amount of patching, vulnerability management, inbound requests, and client requests. You have to manage those two dynamics.

On the technology front, in my career — which some people in this audience might think is long, while others might think it's not that long yet — I've never seen anything move as fast. In a short period of time, we've gone from a nascent technology that we're all excited about to actually operationalizing it. At least in my career, I haven't seen anything cross that divide so quickly. Therefore, I think it's ultimately the biggest change-management exercise, maybe ever. That's really where leaders need to center and focus their time.

In a recent development, DR's Kristina Beek: A lot of people are coming out of college or going into college with the expectation of going into cybersecurity or computer science. AI is changing the field very rapidly. A lot of people are scared that they may not even have a job or that there may not be a place for them in this field. What would you say to that, with the rise of AI?

In a recent development, james Shira: I understand where people get that. I understand how people get that. I think it's understandable, but I think it's wrong. The amount of change across society and industries is significant. It's very difficult for me to chart a course in my head for what isn't going to change. Therefore, I think the opportunity for young professionals is to be the change agents — to deliver the change.

Sources indicate that I think one thing we don't always do well for our young professionals, but need to, is tell them the truth about the adversity of change management. It's hard. It's hard, and it's going to be hard for them. Do I think AI is a job-elimination technology? I don't. But I understand and respect how people might reach that conclusion.

Industry observers note that if you're doing highly repetitive, data-centric activities, that's not, frankly, what you go to college for. Some of us had to do that coming out of college, earning our stripes, but that's not generally what you go to college for. That probably gets changed a lot by AI. Of course. I don't think it's a displacement strategy.

According to recent reports, DR's Kristina Beek: Going back to what you mentioned about how AI is changing things so rapidly, what do you think cybersecurity leaders will spend the most time thinking about three to five years from now? I know that's hard because things are changing so quickly, but what do you see for the future?

James Shira: I think the constants I would expect not to go away are the rate of change, the pace, and the pressure. Therefore, I think you have to find consistency in process and strategic principles, meaning how you manage your strategy shouldn't change. You should find the things in executing the strategy and operationalizing it that don't need to change, because so much around you will be changing.

According to recent reports, in our history, and in at least my part of the 20-year history of IT security and cybersecurity, when there's been a technical change — think cloud, client-server, mobile, or whatever — we've effectively changed every aspect of how we implemented security controls. I'm hoping and working diligently to avoid repeating that pattern in the AI space because I think it just adds too much volume to an already high-intensity, high-volume situation.

Three to five years from now, I'm hoping AI can be a much more consistent enabler of delivering secure outcomes, but we're still learning how to fully operationalize it. Then there's the issue of token costs, which we're not going to get into today, but that has a high degree of relationship to driving the overall security budget, which we're figuring out as we go.

In a recent development, secondly, I don't think most companies will have enough money to build a security program the way we've historically done it, at the size and scale that AI could imply would be required. Third, I think organizations are going to have to shrink their digital footprint as they transform. The good news is that — obviously, hope is not a strategy — AI will hopefully allow us to interact with our systems of state much more efficiently than building applications as the recurring front door to all of our systems, as we've done for the last 10 or 20 years. That ought to have a great benefit in reducing the attack surface, too. I think that's what companies need to do, and I think that's what will look so different in three to five years.

Industry observers note that lastly, I'd say I'm expecting significant societal and industry change, especially in a five-year window. I'm not sure I'm going to have a robot at home, but maybe some of us will. I think physical AI is going to place a significant premium on investment capacity, both on the hardware side and on the adoption and implementation side.

According to recent reports, there are Orwellian views of that, where you could see the doom and gloom. I think there's also a tremendous opportunity. Some countries are not having the birth rates we need. Frankly, there isn't enough reproduction to maintain the number of people in society. So robots in some places in the world are going to be incredibly helpful in allowing us to deliver the things people need in society.

But I'm excited by it. I'll summarize by saying I think the big fundamental choice you have to make every morning when you wake up is to embrace the change, both in yourself and in how you do the job, because the change is almost — I joked with a colleague the other day, and she's a really capable runner while I am not, that this is kind of like being on the treadmill at the speed Annie would go at, not the speed James would go at. Some days I feel like I'm hanging in there, and other days I feel like I'm about to fall off the back of the treadmill. I think everybody just needs to say that's part of this.

Sources indicate that DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. That's great to hear. What has been the most rewarding part of that work, and what do you think will continue to challenge or motivate you, especially in a field where the risks are sometimes really high?

It has been revealed that james Shira: Sure. It's an easy answer for me: It's the people part. It's the team. Every success I've had the privilege of being part of is not a James thing. I had a role, sure, but it's a team thing.

Industry observers note that look, it doesn't always work that way. There are probably people on the team who don't feel they got a fair chance, or who feel something didn't go perfectly. That's the challenge of working in teams of people, because people — me, you, all of us — are not perfect.

In a recent development, but the best days for me are when I see colleagues rise, shine, and do great things, and even leave the organization and go do great things somewhere else. That's pretty awesome. I think that's our opportunity with AI and security. We have to embrace it, try to see the positive in it, and grow through it.

Sources indicate that DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. I so enjoyed this conversation. Thank you so much for joining me today.

Industry observers note that james Shira: Me too. Thanks for your time.

Breaking: Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥.
  • MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon.
  • According to recent reports, stability, and hopefully faster development!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are significant MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

According to recent reports, stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Industry observers note that our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for latest ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

According to recent reports, concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every Cure confirmed a partnership with OpenEvidence on November 16, 2026, to advance latest uses for existing medicines where commercial incentives are lacking, linking AI-supported drug evaluation with specialist input, clinical-trial recruitment and evidence distribution to physicians.

Industry observers note that every Cure estimates that roughly 18,000 diseases are recognized but only about 4,000 have approved treatments, and that more than 300 million people globally have a disease with no FDA-approved treatment. Those figures frame the partnership’s target: promising uses for approved drugs, including generics, that a nonprofit can pursue without a conventional commercial return.

Repurposing builds on existing safety data and manufacturing capacity rather than starting with an entirely new compound. The announcement contrasts that foundation with new-drug development, which can require billions of dollars and more than 10 years. That rationale explains the attraction of repurposing, but it does not establish that any particular candidate will work in a new disease.

Recent findings suggest that every Cure applies data science and AI to evaluate approved drugs against diseases systematically. OpenEvidence will contribute proprietary models and biomedical sources and data, including content from its strategic partnership with Nature journals, to help assess repurposing hypotheses.

Industry observers note that openEvidence will also match individual repurposing programs with physicians who have cared for patients with the relevant disease. For many rare and underserved diseases, only a small number of these physicians exist, making that access a central part of the collaboration.

Sources indicate that “OpenEvidence can help us reach the physicians who care for these patients. Moreover, their firsthand experience will help us ask better research questions and design studies that address what matters most to patients and physicians,” stated Matt Goddeeris, Every Cure’s chief scientific officer.

Industry observers note that once Every Cure identifies a promising opportunity, it remains responsible for generating evidence on whether the treatment is safe and effective in the upcoming disease and for addressing barriers to patient access. OpenEvidence’s role continues as programs move from research into the clinic.

Recent findings suggest that for programs entering clinical trials, OpenEvidence will alert treating physicians when a patient may qualify, leaving the physician to decide whether to pursue a referral. That recruitment support is particularly relevant to rare diseases, where eligible patients can be difficult to locate. As trial results emerge, OpenEvidence will disseminate the findings to physicians at the point of care.

Isabel Ostrer, OpenEvidence’s director of primary care initiatives, described the evidence gap: “Physicians come to OpenEvidence for the best available evidence, but for thousands of diseases, that evidence doesn’t exist yet.”.

In a recent development, every Cure says its approach grew from co-founder and CEO David Fajgenbaum’s experience with idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease. After being told that no options remained, he identified an overactive immune pathway in his blood and tested sirolimus, a drug approved to prevent kidney-transplant rejection that targets the same pathway. He has been in remission for more than 11 years and has advanced 14 additional repurposed drugs.

Sources indicate that openEvidence already works with the National Organization for Rare Disorders on more than 3,000 expert-reviewed rare-disease summaries. The organization claims its platform is used daily, on average, by a majority of U.S. physicians and is free for all verified U.S. clinicians, providing the reach through which it looks to support specialist matching, referrals and dissemination.

In a recent development, the partnership joins that repurposing experience to a national clinical network. Its central test is whether AI-assisted hypotheses, paired with specialist knowledge and physician reach, can become credible trial evidence and accessible treatments for patients who otherwise have few options.

Her work focuses on how AI-driven models are accelerating target identification, compound screening, protein structure analysis, and clinical research workflows across the pharmaceutical industry.

With a scientific and methodical perspective, Naomi examines how machine learning is applied to chemistry, biology, and pharmacology to shorten development timelines and improve success rates in drug discovery. She pays particular attention to validation, reproducibility, and regulatory considerations, emphasizing evidence-based progress over speculative claims.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that.
  • And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

In a recent development, running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

Industry observers note that GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so people can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

In a recent development, we want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

Industry observers note that GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

Industry observers note that we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

According to recent reports, no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

In a recent development, the model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

Sources indicate that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

Sources indicate that transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Industry observers note that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

It has been revealed that transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

Recent findings suggest that that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

It has been revealed that we also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Industry observers note that our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

It has been revealed that the first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

It has been revealed that to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

According to recent reports, these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

Industry observers note that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

It has been revealed that if you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

INFevo announced on November 16, 2026 that it had raised more than RMB 100 million in Pre-A funding to expand its AI virtual-cell models and automated experimental systems, according to investor Xinglian Capital’s announcement. The proceeds will also support deeper collaboration with pharmaceutical companies, hospitals and research institutions.

Xinglian Capital, Prosperity7 Ventures, Huagai Capital, Huakong Fund and DT Capital joined the round. Existing investors Shunwei Capital, HSG and Songhe Capital made additional investments. The financing followed an angel round of tens of millions of yuan in June 2026, making it INFevo’s second in five months; Xinglian described it as a record single-round financing for a Chinese virtual-cell company.

INFevo’s virtual-cell approach is designed to predict cellular responses to drug or genetic interventions before laboratory experiments. Researchers could then compare potential targets, rank candidate molecules and reserve wet-lab capacity for more promising questions. XtalPi, which incubated INFevo, described in a July 16, 2026 announcement how its molecular-design and automated-synthesis capabilities could complement those predictions, creating a chain from molecular generation through cellular-response prediction to experimental validation.

Sources indicate that the OCOO-T paper describes a minimalist flow-matching model whose standard Transformer stack operates directly on continuous gene-expression profiles. Prediction is formulated as continuous-time denoising, while perturbation, dosage and cell-line or cell-type information enter through adaptive layer normalization and in-context tokens.

Recent findings suggest that the authors report state-of-the-art results across the Tahoe100M, Replogle and PBMC benchmarks, covering chemical, genetic and cytokine perturbations. The model also scales to long transcriptional profiles by patching and depatching cellular contexts.

Beyond a single model, INFevo is building what it calls recursive scientific discovery: retaining scientific questions, hypotheses, analytical methods and experimental results so they can inform later hypotheses, experiment designs and candidate selection. Its automated wet-lab system covers cell culture, perturbation and multi-omics measurement. Model predictions help choose experiments, while the resulting data test those predictions and feed subsequent model improvements.

It has been revealed that the Popper Project addresses the hypothesis side of that research process. Named after philosopher Karl Popper, it uses research agents and professional databases to generate, challenge and refine testable hypotheses, displaying traceable reasoning chains, evidence gaps and proposed experiments. Its Karl Workbench has entered beta testing, with research records, accumulated evidence, outputs, supervision and iterative-improvement functions that let researchers review judgments and resume earlier tasks.

Xinglian reported that an October 2026 retest using SciAgentArena placed Karl Workbench first overall in both single-cell and spatial omics when running on DeepSeek. The benchmark comprises approximately 200 stepwise-verified tasks across drug discovery, single-cell omics, spatial omics, electronic health records and genetics. It separates agent execution from evaluation and assesses data analysis, optimization, discovery and validity checking.

In a recent development, sciAgentArena’s authors found that no single agent dominated across tasks and domains. Current systems performed unevenly, had difficulty with novel discovery and self-directed exploration, and tended to execute requests even when the scientific premise was invalid. That wider record makes the scope of INFevo’s reported result crucial: the retest concerns DeepSeek in two omics categories, rather than a general lead across scientific research.

INFevo is also participating in a Beijing key laboratory led by Peking University First Hospital that focuses on liver, biliary and pancreatic tumor organoid culture and intelligent diagnosis and treatment. The collaboration’s stated aim is to connect clinical questions, patient-derived organoid models, drug screening, AI analysis and clinical validation. Model predictions and organoid experiments are intended to inform one another, bringing the virtual-cell system into contact with patient-derived clinical samples.

It has been revealed that co-founder Yalong Zhao noted the financing would support the foundation-model and automated-experiment infrastructure and accelerate the recursive-discovery system. Lipeng Lai, another INFevo co-founder, is also XtalPi’s co-founder and chief innovation officer.

It has been revealed that the upcoming capital gives INFevo resources to expand both sides of that system: computational prediction and automated validation. The consequential test is whether developer-reported benchmark results and beta research tools can become repeatable performance on patient-derived samples and in pharmaceutical research workflows.

How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible
